courses.title: Ch 6 · My Childhood
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam's memories of growing up in Rameswaram — his family, his friends across religions, two teachers who showed prejudice and courage, and his first earnings.
outcomes: Learners can describe Kalam's family and early influences
Learners can explain the incidents of prejudice and how they were resolved
Learners can discuss secularism and social harmony
Learners can answer board questions with textual detail

scenes.text: In a big old house of limestone and brick in Rameswaram, a boy grows up in a loving, simple family.
His three best friends come from priestly Hindu families. Nobody at home thinks it unusual.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
**Avul Pakir Jainulabdeen Abdul Kalam** was born in **Rameswaram** (in the then Madras State, now Tamil Nadu) into a middle-class **Tamil Muslim** family. His father **Jainulabdeen** had little formal education or wealth but great **wisdom** and generosity; his mother **Ashiamma** was an ideal helpmate who fed many outsiders every day. They lived in an **ancestral house** built in the middle of the 19th century, of limestone and brick. The family lived simply, but provided all necessities.

Kalam's three close childhood friends were **Ramanadha Sastry**, **Aravindan** and **Sivaprakasan**, all from orthodox Hindu Brahmin families. As children they never felt any difference because of religion. Ramanadha Sastry was the son of **Pakshi Lakshmana Sastry**, the high priest of the **Rameswaram temple**. Kalam's family arranged boats with a special platform for carrying idols during the annual **Shri Sita Rama Kalyanam** ceremony. His mother and grandmother told bedtime stories from the **Ramayana** and the life of the Prophet.

steps.title: People in Kalam's childhood
steps.body:
- **Jainulabdeen** – father; wise, honest, self-disciplined.
- **Ashiamma** – mother; generous.
- **Ramanadha Sastry, Aravindan, Sivaprakasan** – friends.
- **Pakshi Lakshmana Sastry** – high priest, father of Ramanadha.
- **Samsuddin** – cousin, newspaper distributor.
- **Sivasubramania Iyer** – science teacher.
- **Ahmed Jallaluddin** – later his brother-in-law (Kalam does not dwell on him here).

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Describe Kalam's parents. (3 marks)** His father Jainulabdeen had little education or wealth but was wise, generous and disciplined; his mother Ashiamma was an ideal helpmate who fed many outsiders daily. Both gave Kalam a secure, value-rich childhood.

**Q2. What shows religious harmony in Kalam's childhood? (2 marks)** His best friends were Hindu Brahmins; his family helped in the Sita Rama Kalyanam festival; he heard stories from the Ramayana and from the life of the Prophet.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Kalam's father's name is **Jainulabdeen**; mother **Ashiamma**.
- Rameswaram was in the **Madras State** then (now Tamil Nadu).
- His three friends were Hindus, not Muslims.

activity.prompt: Match the person to the description

quiz.why: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam was born in Rameswaram, an island town in Tamil Nadu. Ramanathapuram is the district headquarters where he later studied.
Kalam's mother was Ashiamma. She was a kind, generous woman who fed many people every day.
Kalam's three close friends came from orthodox Hindu Brahmin families, although he was Muslim. Their friendship shows communal harmony.

quiz.q: His family helped in which ceremony?
quiz.why: Kalam's family helped in the Shri Sita Rama Kalyanam ceremony by arranging boats to carry the idols to the marriage site. It shows a shared community life.

quiz.q: Kalam's ancestral house was made of:
quiz.why: Kalam's ancestral house was built of limestone and brick. It was a fairly large house on Mosque Street in Rameswaram.

lessons.title: First earnings and the Second World War

scenes.text: 1939: suddenly tamarind seeds are in demand. Young Kalam collects them and sells them to a shop for an anna a day.
Then his cousin gives him a job catching newspaper bundles thrown from a moving train.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
When the **Second World War** broke out in **1939**, Kalam was about eight. For some reason, there was a sudden demand for **tamarind seeds**. He collected the seeds and sold them to a provision shop on Mosque Street — earning **one anna** a day.

The train halt at Rameswaram station was suspended because of the war, so newspapers had to be bundled and **thrown out from the moving train** on the Rameswaram–Dhanuskodi route. His cousin **Samsuddin**, who distributed newspapers, needed help to catch the bundles, and Kalam filled the slot. He says he earned his **first wages** this way, and remembers the pride half a century later.

Kalam notes that every child is born, with some inherited characteristics, into a specific socio-economic and emotional environment, and is shaped by authority figures. From his father he learned **honesty and self-discipline**; from his mother **faith in goodness and deep kindness** — as did his three brothers and sister.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. How did Kalam earn his first wages? (2 marks)** By helping his cousin Samsuddin catch newspaper bundles thrown from the moving train during WWII.

**Q2. What qualities did Kalam inherit from his parents? (2 marks)** Honesty and self-discipline from his father; faith in goodness and deep kindness from his mother.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The first earning was from **tamarind seeds** (one anna a day), but he calls the newspaper job his **first wages**.
- WWII broke out in **1939**.

steps.title: What is an anna?
steps.body: An **anna** was a unit of currency; 16 annas made one rupee (before decimal coinage was introduced in 1957).

statements.s: Kalam sold tamarind seeds for one anna a day.
Newspapers were thrown from the moving train because the halt was suspended.
Kalam's cousin was Ramanadha Sastry.
16 annas made one rupee.

quiz.why: The Second World War broke out in 1939. 1914 was the start of the First World War.

quiz.q: What did Kalam collect and sell?
quiz.why: During the war Kalam collected tamarind seeds and sold them to a provision shop. He earned a little money for the family this way.

quiz.q: Who helped Kalam earn his first wages?
quiz.why: Samsuddin, Kalam's cousin, helped him earn his first wages by letting him help to catch the newspaper bundles thrown from the train. Aravindan was a friend.
From his father Kalam inherited honesty and self-discipline. His father had no great wealth, but good values.

quiz.q: How many annas made a rupee?
quiz.why: A rupee was made up of 16 annas, in the old currency. So 16 annas = 1 rupee.

scenes.text: A new teacher sees a Muslim boy in a cap sitting next to the priest's son and orders him to the back bench.
The priest hears of it and tells the teacher to apologise — or leave the island.

steps.title: The new teacher (fifth standard)
steps.body:
When Kalam was in the **fifth standard** at the Rameswaram Elementary School, a **new teacher** came. Kalam wore a cap marking him as a Muslim and always sat in the front row beside Ramanadha Sastry, who wore a sacred thread. The teacher could not stand a Hindu priest's son sitting with a Muslim boy, and sent Kalam to the **back bench**. Both boys were sad; Ramanadha wept.

When **Lakshmana Sastry** heard, he summoned the teacher and told him in front of the boys that he should not spread **social inequality and communal intolerance** in the minds of innocent children. He asked the teacher either to **apologise** or **quit the school and the island**. The teacher regretted his behaviour and **reformed**.

steps.title: Sivasubramania Iyer's dinner
steps.body: Kalam's **science teacher Sivasubramania Iyer**, though an orthodox Brahmin with a very conservative wife, was something of a rebel who wanted to break social barriers. He invited Kalam home for a meal. His wife was horrified at a Muslim boy eating in her ritually pure kitchen and refused to serve. Iyer, unperturbed, **served Kalam with his own hands** and sat beside him to eat. He told Kalam that when you decide to change the system, such problems have to be confronted. When Kalam came again the next week, Iyer's **wife herself took him into the kitchen and served him food**.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. How did Lakshmana Sastry deal with the new teacher? (3 marks)** He summoned him, said he must not spread social inequality and communal intolerance among innocent children, and asked him to apologise or leave the school and island. The teacher regretted it and changed.

**Q2. How did Sivasubramania Iyer's wife change? (2 marks)** At first she refused to serve Kalam; a week later she personally served him in her kitchen — her prejudice gave way.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The **new teacher** moved Kalam; the **science teacher** (Iyer) invited him to dinner — don't mix them.
- It was Lakshmana Sastry (the priest), not Kalam's father, who confronted the teacher.

activity.prompt: Prejudice or courage?

items.text: New teacher sends Kalam to the back bench
Lakshmana Sastry asks teacher to apologise or leave
Iyer's wife refuses to serve Kalam at first
Iyer serves Kalam with his own hands
Iyer's wife later serves Kalam herself

quiz.q: In which standard was Kalam moved to the back bench?
quiz.why: Kalam was moved to the back bench in the fifth standard, when a new teacher could not accept a Muslim boy sitting beside Ramanadha Sastry, a Brahmin priest's son.
Lakshmana Sastry, the high priest of the Rameswaram temple, confronted the new teacher. He told him that he was spreading social inequality and communal intolerance.

quiz.q: The new teacher was asked to:
options: Apologise or leave the school and island
quiz.why: The high priest told the new teacher to apologise or to quit the school and the island. The teacher then reformed.

quiz.q: Who served Kalam the first time at Iyer's house?
quiz.why: Iyer himself served Kalam the food on his next visit, as his wife was willing to accept him by then. He showed courage in breaking the old custom.
Sivasubramania Iyer was Kalam's science teacher. He encouraged Kalam and invited him home for a meal.

lessons.title: Leaving home; themes and answer writing

scenes.text: After the war, young Kalam asks his father's permission to leave Rameswaram to study at the district headquarters, Ramanathapuram.
His father agrees, reminding his mother that children have their own destinies to follow.

steps.title: Leaving Rameswaram
steps.body: After the war ended, Kalam asked his father's permission to study at **Ramanathapuram**, the district headquarters. His father agreed and, quoting the poet **Khalil Gibran**, told his reluctant mother that children are not their parents' possessions; they have their own thoughts and destinies. Parents must let them grow. He told Kalam that, like a seagull flying alone across the sea, he must leave home to grow. (Paraphrased.) The chapter also notes that India's **Independence (1947)** brought hope of a new society.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Secularism and religious harmony**
- **Role of good teachers and elders** in fighting prejudice
- **Simple living, high values**
- **Courage to change society** (Iyer, Lakshmana Sastry)
- **Letting children grow** (father's wisdom)

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. 'Kalam's childhood shows how good people can defeat prejudice.' Explain. (6 marks)**
Kalam grew up in a home that respected all faiths; his best friends were Brahmin boys and his family served at the Sita Rama Kalyanam festival. When a new teacher sent him to the back bench because he was Muslim, the high priest Lakshmana Sastry rebuked him and made him apologise. Similarly, science teacher Sivasubramania Iyer broke the barrier by inviting Kalam home and serving him himself; his conservative wife later served Kalam with her own hands. These elders showed courage and compassion, proving that social inequality can be overcome when good people act.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Kalam went to **Ramanathapuram**, not Madras, after the war.
- The quotation about children is attributed to **Khalil Gibran**.

activity.prompt: Have you ever seen someone treated unfairly because of religion, caste, gender or background? What could you do, like Lakshmana Sastry or Iyer?
activity.hint: Think of small brave acts: sitting with someone left out, speaking to a teacher, inviting someone home.

quiz.q: Kalam left home to study at:
quiz.why: Kalam left home to study at Ramanathapuram, the district headquarters. His father encouraged this.
Kalam's father quoted Khalil Gibran, saying that children have their own destiny. He let Kalam leave to grow.
A central theme of the chapter is communal harmony, as shown by the friendships and the teachers' action. It is not about sports or wealth.
A.P.J. Abdul Kalam wrote 'My Childhood', an extract from his autobiography Wings of Fire. Vikram Seth and Ruskin Bond wrote other works.

quiz.q: The father compared Kalam's leaving to a:
quiz.why: The father compared Kalam's going away to a seagull flying alone, as the seagull flies alone, so must children seek their own path.

questions.q: My Childhood is an excerpt from Kalam's autobiography:
questions.why: 'My Childhood' is an excerpt from Kalam's autobiography Wings of Fire. India 2020 and Ignited Minds are different books.

questions.q: Kalam's father was:
questions.why: Kalam's father was Jainulabdeen, a boat owner and imam. Ashiamma was his mother.

questions.q: Kalam's hometown:
questions.why: Kalam's hometown was Rameswaram, a pilgrim island town. Madurai and Thanjavur are other places.

questions.q: Kalam earned his first wages by:
questions.why: Kalam earned his first wages by helping to distribute newspapers, catching the bundles thrown from the moving train. Samsuddin was his helper.

questions.q: Which friend was the son of the temple priest?
questions.why: Ramanadha Sastry, Kalam's close friend, was the son of the head priest of the Rameswaram temple. Samsuddin was his cousin.

questions.q: Kalam wore a cap which marked him as:
questions.why: Kalam wore a cap, which marked him out as a Muslim boy. This is why the new teacher objected to his seat.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The new teacher reformed. Reason (R): Lakshmana Sastry asked him to apologise or leave.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The high priest told the teacher to apologise or leave, so the teacher reformed.

questions.q: Why was the train halt suspended?
questions.why: The train halt at Rameswaram was suspended because of the Second World War. Newspapers then came by a moving train.

questions.q: What did Iyer say about changing the system?
questions.why: Iyer said that such social problems must be confronted and not avoided, if the system is to change. He was a rebel against old customs.

questions.q: Which statement best describes Kalam's parents?
questions.why: Kalam's parents were simple, wise and generous, with strong values. They were not rich or careless.

questions.q: If Kalam earned one anna a day for 32 days, how many rupees did he earn (16 annas = 1 rupee)?
questions.why: 32 annas ÷ 16 annas per rupee = 2 rupees. One anna a day for 32 days gives 32 annas.

questions.q: Case: A school seats children by caste. Which character's action shows the right response?
questions.why: Lakshmana Sastry confronted the discrimination in the school and made the teacher change. Others did not take such a stand.

questions.q: Which change happened in Iyer's wife?
questions.why: Iyer's wife changed from prejudiced to accepting, as she served Kalam herself the next time. It shows a change in attitude.

questions.q: Why does Kalam remember his first wages with pride even after fifty years?
options: It was earned through his own effort and helped the family
questions.why: Kalam's first wages were earned by his own effort and helped the family, so he remembers them with pride even after fifty years. It was the dignity of labour.

questions.q: The father's words about children 'having their own destinies' show:
options: Wisdom and respect for a child's growth
questions.why: The father's words that children have their own destinies show wisdom and respect for a child's growth. He allowed Kalam to go and seek his path.

Learners can compare the two achievers
Learners can write character sketches and board answers

scenes.text: In a Haryana village where girls marry early, a sixteen-year-old refuses to marry and insists on studying.
Years later, she stands on top of Mount Everest — not once, but twice.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
**Santosh Yadav** was born in **Joniyawas**, a village in **Rewari district, Haryana**, a society where sons were preferred. She was the sixth child and only daughter. She chose to walk her own path — wearing shorts instead of traditional dress, and insisting on education. At **16**, she refused to marry and said she would study first, paying her own fees if needed. Her parents finally agreed.

She went to **Jaipur**, studied at **Maharani College**, and from her hostel saw people climbing the **Aravalli** hills. Curious, she joined them and found her passion. She enrolled at the **Nehru Institute of Mountaineering, Uttarkashi**, paying fees from her own savings.

She climbed **Mount Everest in May 1992** (at about 20) and again in **May 1993**, becoming the **first woman in the world to climb Everest twice**. On the first climb she showed concern for others, sharing oxygen with a fellow climber who was struggling. She was awarded the **Padma Shri**. She also cared for the environment, collecting and bringing down a large amount of garbage from the Himalayas.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. How did Santosh show determination early in life? (3 marks)** She refused traditional dress; insisted on going to a good school in Delhi; at 16 refused early marriage, saying she would earn to pay her fees if needed.

**Q2. What made her first woman to climb Everest twice? (2 marks)** She scaled Everest in May 1992 and again in May 1993.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- She is from **Haryana** (Rewari), not Rajasthan; she studied in Jaipur.
- Her climbs were in **1992 and 1993** — within twelve months.

activity.prompt: Order Santosh Yadav's journey

events.text: Grows up in Joniyawas, Rewari
Refuses early marriage to study
Watches climbers on the Aravallis from her hostel
Trains at the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering
First Everest ascent
Second Everest ascent — a world record

quiz.why: Santosh Yadav was born in Rewari, Haryana. She is a well-known mountaineer.
Santosh studied at Maharani College in Jaipur. She was already an independent young woman there.
Santosh trained at the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering at Uttarkashi. It is a leading mountaineering school.
Santosh climbed Everest in 1992 and again in 1993, becoming the first woman to do it twice. This is an unusual achievement.
Santosh Yadav received the Padma Shri, a national honour. The Nobel and Bharat Ratna are not hers.

story.title: Nine years old, far from home

scenes.text: A nine-year-old girl from Siberia flies to the USA with her father to train in tennis. Her mother cannot come because of visa rules.
She trains hard, feels lonely, but never quits. By 18 she is the world's number one.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
**Maria Sharapova** was born in **Siberia**, Russia. At **nine**, she was sent to the **USA** with her father **Yuri** to train at a tennis academy in Florida; her mother could not accompany them because of visa restrictions. She was lonely and missed her mother; older trainees bullied her, waking her late at night to tidy the room. But she stayed focused on her goal, saying she was very determined and did not want to give up.

Her sacrifice paid off: she became one of the world's top players and reached **world number one** in **2005**, at **18**. She enjoyed fashion, singing and dancing, read novels, and loved wealth and fame earned through hard work. She is described as competitive and confident.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What hardships did Maria face in the USA? (3 marks)** She was separated from her mother for two years; she was lonely; older girls bullied her and made her clean the room; training was hard and long.

**Q2. How did she cope? (2 marks)** By focusing on her goal, believing in herself and refusing to quit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- She went to the USA at **nine**, not as a teenager.
- She became world No. 1 in **2005**.

steps.title: Qualities of achievers
steps.body: Determination · hard work · courage to break norms · self-belief · sacrifice · focus on goals · resilience in loneliness and setbacks.

statements.s: Maria went to the USA at the age of nine.
Her mother went with her.
She became world No. 1 at 18.
Maria was born in Moscow.

quiz.why: Maria Sharapova was born in Siberia, in Russia. She later became a famous tennis player.

quiz.q: She went to the USA with her:
quiz.why: Maria went to the USA with her father Yuri. Her mother could not join them at first.
Maria became world number one in 2005, when she was 18. She had worked hard for years to get there.
Maria's mother could not go with her because of visa restrictions. This meant the two were separated for two years.
Maria succeeded through determination and hard work, along with focus. It was not luck alone or wealth.

scenes.text: For a school 'Women Achievers' wall, Kavya puts Santosh and Maria side by side.
She writes: 'Different worlds, same fire.'

steps.title: Compare the two
steps.body:
- **Background**: Santosh – rural Haryana, conservative society; Maria – Siberia, moved to USA at 9.
- **Challenge**: Santosh – social norms (early marriage, gender roles); Maria – loneliness, separation, bullying.
- **Field**: mountaineering vs tennis.
- **Common**: determination, hard work, self-belief, sacrifice, breaking barriers.

steps.title: Solved character sketch: Santosh Yadav
steps.body: Determined and independent — refused early marriage; hard-working — paid her own fees; courageous — took up mountaineering; caring — shared oxygen with a fellow climber; environmentally aware — cleaned up Himalayan garbage; role model for girls in rural India.

steps.title: Solved character sketch: Maria Sharapova
steps.body: Ambitious and competitive; resilient — endured loneliness at nine; disciplined — long training hours; confident; candid about loving success and the rewards of hard work.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up which achiever faced which challenge.
- Writing only praise without examples.

activity.prompt: Santosh, Maria or both?

quiz.why: Both Santosh and Maria were determined to reach their goals despite difficulties. They did not come from wealth or give in to fear.
Santosh's main challenge was social norms about girls, which many tried to impose on her. She stood against them.
Maria's main challenge was loneliness and separation from her mother, living in a new country. It was not mountains or early marriage.

quiz.q: Which shows Santosh's concern for nature?
options: Bringing down garbage from the Himalayas
quiz.why: Santosh's concern for nature is shown by her bringing down garbage from the Himalayas. It shows she cared about the environment.
A character sketch should include traits with examples from the text. A mere date list or praise is not enough.

scenes.text: Amit is asked to give a speech on 'Never Give Up' at Sports Day.
He uses Santosh and Maria as examples and gets loud applause.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **expedition**: a journey with a purpose (e.g., to climb a mountain)
- **summit**: top of a mountain
- **altitude**: height above sea level
- **resolve**: firm decision
- **ecological**: related to the environment
- **prodigy**: a young person with exceptional talent
- **feisty**: lively and determined

steps.title: Writing link: speech
steps.body: Speech format: greeting ('Good morning, respected Principal, teachers and friends') → introduce topic → 3 points with examples → conclusion and call to action → 'Thank you'. Length: 120–150 words.

steps.title: Solved paragraph
steps.body: **'Grit beats talent'**: Santosh Yadav and Maria Sharapova both faced obstacles that could have stopped them. Santosh fought social pressure to marry early; Maria lived far from her mother as a child. Neither gave up. Their success shows that steady hard work and self-belief matter more than luck.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the greeting and thank-you in a speech.
- Summit (top) vs altitude (height).

activity.prompt: Match the word to its meaning

quiz.why: 'Summit' means the top of a mountain. It is the highest point.
A speech begins with a greeting to the audience, like 'Respected principal, teachers and friends'. A date or 'Dear diary' belongs to other forms.
An expedition is a purposeful journey, often one of exploration, such as to climb a mountain. It is not a party or a game.
'Resolve' here means a firm decision or determination. It does not mean doubt or weakness.

quiz.q: Which line suits a 'Never Give Up' speech?
options: Hard work and self-belief help us cross obstacles
quiz.why: A 'Never Give Up' speech should say that hard work and self-belief help us overcome obstacles. Quitting or relying on luck goes against it.

questions.q: Santosh Yadav is a:
questions.why: Santosh Yadav is a mountaineer, famous for climbing Everest twice. She is not a tennis player or a singer.

questions.q: Maria Sharapova plays:
questions.why: Maria Sharapova plays tennis. She became the world number one in 2005.

questions.q: Santosh climbed Everest:
questions.why: Santosh climbed Everest twice, in 1992 and 1993. She was the first woman to do so.

questions.q: Santosh first saw climbers on the:
questions.why: Santosh first saw climbers on the Aravallis near Jaipur, which inspired her. She later went on to the Himalayas.

questions.q: Maria moved to the USA at the age of:
questions.why: Maria moved to the USA at the age of nine, to train as a tennis player. She went with her father.

questions.q: Santosh was the only daughter among:
questions.why: Santosh was the sixth child and the only daughter among six children. This made her fight even harder for freedom.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Santosh paid her own fees at times. Reason (R): She was determined to study despite family pressure.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Santosh was so determined to study, despite family pressure, that she paid her own fees at times.

questions.q: Which statement is FALSE?
options: Maria's mother lived with her in the USA from the start
Maria was bullied by older trainees
questions.why: Maria's mother could not live with her in the USA at first because of visa restrictions, so that statement is false. The other statements are true.

questions.q: Santosh showed compassion on Everest by:
options: Sharing oxygen with a struggling climber
questions.why: On Everest Santosh shared her oxygen with a struggling climber, which shows compassion. She did not abandon the team.

questions.q: Both achievers challenge the idea that:
questions.why: Both achievers challenge the idea that circumstances decide destiny, since they rose above difficulties. They show that hard work pays.

questions.q: If Santosh first climbed Everest in 1992 at about 20, in which year was she born (approx.)?
questions.why: Birth year ≈ 1992 − 20 = 1972, so the nearest answer is 1972. Sources vary slightly.

questions.q: Maria reached No. 1 at 18 in 2005. In which year was she born?
questions.why: Birth year = 2005 − 18 = 1987. The other years do not match her age.

questions.q: Case: A girl in your village is being pressured to marry at 16. Which part of Santosh's story is most relevant?
options: Her refusal to marry early and choosing education
questions.why: Santosh refused to marry early and chose education, which is most relevant to a girl facing early marriage pressure. Note that the legal minimum age of marriage for women in India is 18.

questions.q: What does 'Reach for the Top' symbolise?
options: Striving for the highest goals in any field
questions.why: 'Reach for the Top' stands for striving for the highest goals in any field, not just climbing. It is a symbolic title.

questions.q: Which quality is most responsible for both achievers' success?
questions.why: Resilience and dedication were most responsible for both women's success. Luck, connections or inheritance did not play that role.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Kathmandu
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Vikram Seth's travel account of Kathmandu — the bustling Pashupatinath temple, the calm Baudhnath stupa, the busy streets, and a flute seller whose music touches the writer.
outcomes: Learners can describe Pashupatinath and Baudhnath and contrast them
Learners can describe the city's sights and sounds
Learners can explain the writer's reflections on the flute
Learners can write descriptive paragraphs and travelogue entries

scenes.text: At Pashupatinath, a traveller is pushed by crowds, sees monkeys fight and priests chant by the river.
At Baudhnath, a few kilometres away, he finds a vast, quiet stupa where time seems to slow down.

steps.title: Pashupatinath
steps.body: The writer, **Vikram Seth**, visits **Pashupatinath**, a Hindu temple of Lord Shiva (as Pashupati) in Kathmandu. Only Hindus are allowed inside the temple. The atmosphere is one of **feverish confusion**: priests, hawkers, devotees, tourists, cows, monkeys and pigeons all crowd the area. Westerners in saffron are turned away by a soldier. A fight breaks out among monkeys; one jumps onto a shivalinga. People bathe in and wash in the **Bagmati** river; a corpse is being cremated on its banks; a woman washes clothes; and someone throws dead flowers into the river. A small shrine half protrudes from the stone platform on the riverbank; it is believed that when it fully emerges, the goddess inside will escape, and the evil period of the **Kaliyug** will end on earth.

steps.title: Baudhnath
steps.body: In contrast, the **Baudhnath stupa**, a Buddhist shrine, has an air of **stillness**. Its immense white dome is ringed by a road with small shops run by Tibetan immigrants — selling felt bags, Tibetan prints and silver jewellery. There is no crowd; it is a **haven of quietness** in the busy streets.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Contrast the atmosphere at Pashupatinath and Baudhnath. (3 marks)** Pashupatinath: feverish confusion — crowds, priests, hawkers, monkeys, rituals by the Bagmati. Baudhnath: calm, still, quiet; few people, a peaceful white dome.

**Q2. What belief is linked to the shrine on the Bagmati? (2 marks)** When the small shrine fully emerges from the platform, the goddess will escape and the evil Kaliyug will end.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Pashupatinath is **Hindu**; Baudhnath is **Buddhist**.
- The river is the **Bagmati**, not the Ganga.

activity.prompt: Which place is described?

items.text: Feverish confusion of devotees and hawkers

quiz.why: Pashupatinath is a temple of Shiva, who is worshipped there as Pashupati, the Lord of animals. It is a Hindu temple.
The Bagmati river flows near the Pashupatinath temple. It is considered sacred.
Baudhnath is a Buddhist stupa, a large dome-shaped shrine. It is not a church, mosque or Hindu temple.
At Baudhnath the atmosphere is calm and still, in contrast to the busy streets. It feels peaceful.
Vikram Seth wrote 'Kathmandu', taken from his travel book Heaven Lake. Kalam and Ruskin Bond wrote other works.

lessons.title: The city and the flute seller

scenes.text: In a crowded Kathmandu square, a man holds a pole hung with bamboo flutes, like a porcupine.
He plays slowly, absorbed; the writer stops, entranced, thinking of flutes all over the world.

steps.title: Kathmandu's streets
steps.body: Kathmandu is **vivid, mercenary and religious**: small shrines on narrow, busy streets; fruit sellers, flute sellers and hawkers of postcards; shops selling Western cosmetics, film rolls, chocolate and copper utensils; radios, car horns, bicycle bells, vendors calling out. The writer eats a bar of marzipan, a corn-on-the-cob roasted in a charcoal brazier, drinks Coca-Cola and reads a comic and a Reader's Digest. He decides to return home by **bus and train** rather than fly (he is tired and homesick).

steps.title: Reflections on the flute
steps.body: Near his hotel, a flute seller stands with a pole carrying about **fifty or sixty** bamboo flutes, looking like a porcupine. Every now and then he plays a few notes, slowly and meditatively, without hawking. The writer is fascinated. He reflects that almost every culture has its own flute — the reed neh, the recorder, the Japanese shakuhachi, the deep bansuri of Hindustani music, the clear flutes of South America, high-pitched Chinese flutes. The flute's music is closest to the human voice, because it is breathed into — moving, intimate, uniting people across cultures.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why does the writer compare the flute pole to a porcupine? (2 marks)** Because the many flutes sticking out from the pole look like a porcupine's quills.

**Q2. What does the writer feel about flute music? (3 marks)** He finds it enchanting and universal — every culture has a flute; it is the closest to the human voice because it requires breath; it is intimate and unites people.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The flute seller does **not** shout to sell — he plays calmly.
- The writer decides to return by **bus and train**, not by plane.

activity.prompt: Match the flute to its culture (as listed in the chapter)

quiz.q: The flute pole is compared to a:
quiz.why: The pole of flutes is compared to a porcupine, because the flutes stick out like quills. It makes the seller look prickly.

quiz.q: How many flutes are on the pole (approx.)?
quiz.why: The flute seller carried about 50 or 60 flutes on his pole. This is why he looks like a porcupine.

quiz.q: Why is flute music close to the human voice?
quiz.why: Flute music is close to the human voice because it is made by human breath. This gives it a voice-like quality.
The writer returns home by bus and train, travelling overland. He did not fly.
Kathmandu is described as vivid, mercenary and religious, with temples and commerce side by side. It is not empty or silent.

scenes.text: On a family trip to Varanasi, Tanya notes the sounds of bells, smells of incense and the colours of boats.
Back home, she writes a vivid travelogue like Vikram Seth.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **feverish confusion**: frantic, chaotic activity
- **mercenary**: working for money (commercial)
- **haven**: a safe, peaceful place
- **hawker**: a person who sells goods on the street
- **brazier**: a container for burning charcoal
- **enchanted/entranced**: charmed, spellbound

steps.title: How to write a vivid description
steps.body: Use the **five senses** (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch). Contrast (noise vs calm). Use specific nouns ('corn roasted on a charcoal brazier') and strong adjectives. Organise by space (from entrance to inside) or time.

steps.title: Solved descriptive paragraph
steps.body: **A busy market at evening**: The market wakes as the sun sets. Strings of yellow bulbs glow above carts piled with oranges and guavas. Vendors call out prices, scooters honk, and the smell of frying samosas drifts from a corner stall. A flute seller plays a soft tune, and for a moment the noise seems to pause.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Listing things without sensory detail.
- Using the same adjective ('nice') repeatedly.

activity.prompt: Fill in with words from the chapter
activity.text: Pashupatinath had an atmosphere of feverish ___, while Baudhnath was a ___ of quietness.

quiz.why: 'Haven' means a safe, peaceful place, a refuge. It is the opposite of a storm.
A hawker is a street seller who goes about selling goods. It is not a bird or a priest.
A vivid description uses the five senses, like sight, sound and smell, to make a scene come alive. It is not just facts or numbers.
Here 'mercenary' means commercial, money-minded. It does not mean peaceful or religious.
A brazier is a container for burning charcoal, used for roasting or heating. It is not for water or music.

scenes.text: After days of travel, the writer lies in his room and longs for home.
He decides: no plane — he wants to see the plains slowly by bus and train.

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. How does Vikram Seth bring Kathmandu alive for the reader? (6 marks)**
Seth uses vivid sensory detail and contrast. At Pashupatinath he describes the crowd, priests, monkeys fighting and rituals by the Bagmati — creating 'feverish confusion'. At Baudhnath he paints stillness: the white dome and quiet Tibetan shops. The streets are full of sounds — radios, horns, vendors — and tastes of marzipan and roasted corn. Finally, the flute seller's music becomes a moment of reflection on flutes across cultures. The mix of observation and reflection makes the city alive.

steps.title: Solved extract (paraphrased)
steps.body:
**Passage (paraphrased):** A small shrine sticks halfway out of the stone platform on the riverbank. When it emerges fully, the goddess inside will escape and the evil period of the Kaliyug will end.
(a) Where is the shrine? → On the bank of the Bagmati at Pashupatinath.
(b) What will happen when it emerges? → The goddess will escape; Kaliyug will end.
(c) What does this show? → Local faith and legend.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Don't write Kathmandu is in India — it is the capital of **Nepal**.
- Keep travel answers in **past tense** (the writer's visit).

steps.title: Travelogue format
steps.body: Title · place and date · arrival impressions · 2–3 highlights with senses · a reflection · closing feeling.

statements.s: Kathmandu is the capital of Nepal.
The writer flew back to Delhi.
The flute seller shouted loudly to attract buyers.
Westerners in saffron were stopped at Pashupatinath.

quiz.why: Kathmandu is the capital of Nepal. Bhutan's capital is Thimphu.
The writer's main technique is vivid description and contrast, as with the busy temple and the calm stupa. He does not use poetry or statistics.
The shops around Baudhnath were run by Tibetan immigrants. They sold things to visitors.

quiz.q: When the shrine emerges fully, according to belief:
quiz.why: According to the legend, when the shrine emerges fully, Kaliyug will end. It is a belief about the shrine.
A travelogue usually ends with a reflection or a feeling, as the writer thinks over the journey. It does not end with a map or bill.

questions.q: 'Kathmandu' is a:
questions.why: 'Kathmandu' is a travelogue extract, an account of the writer's travel. It is not a biography, poem or play.

questions.q: Pashupatinath is sacred to:
questions.why: Pashupatinath is sacred to Hindus, as a Shiva temple. Baudhnath is for Buddhists.

questions.q: Baudhnath is sacred to:
questions.why: Baudhnath is sacred to Buddhists, as a stupa. It is not a Hindu or Muslim place.

questions.q: Which river flows by Pashupatinath?
questions.why: The Bagmati river flows by the Pashupatinath temple. The other rivers do not flow there.

questions.q: The flute seller looks like a porcupine because of:
options: The flutes sticking out of his pole
questions.why: The flute seller looks like a porcupine because of the flutes sticking out from his pole, like quills. It has nothing to do with his hair or coat.

questions.q: Which is a flute mentioned from Japan?
questions.why: The shakuhachi is the Japanese flute named in the text. Neh is Arabic and bansuri Indian.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Baudhnath felt like a haven. Reason (R): It was calm and uncrowded compared to the busy streets.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Baudhnath was calm and uncrowded compared with the busy streets, so it felt like a haven.

questions.q: Why did the writer choose bus and train?
options: Cheaper and he was homesick, wanting to go home overland
questions.why: The writer was homesick and tired, so he chose the overland route by bus and train, which was cheaper. It was not due to banned planes.

questions.q: Which best describes the writer's tone?
questions.why: The writer's tone is observant and reflective, as he notes what he sees and thinks about it. He is not angry or sarcastic.

questions.q: What unites flutes across cultures, according to the writer?
options: Breath gives them a human, voice-like quality
questions.why: Flutes everywhere are made to be played with breath, which gives them a human, voice-like quality. That is what unites them across cultures.

questions.q: If the flute seller had 60 flutes and sold 15, what fraction remained?
questions.why: If 15 of 60 were sold, 60 − 15 = 45 remain, and 45/60 = 3/4. So three-fourths remain.

questions.q: Case: A student wants to describe a temple fair. What should she learn from Seth?
options: Use sensory detail, contrast and personal reflection
questions.why: From Seth, a student can learn to use sensory detail, contrast and personal reflection. Avoiding adjectives or using only facts would make it dull.

questions.q: What does the monkey jumping on a shivalinga suggest?
options: The chaotic, crowded atmosphere at Pashupatinath
questions.why: The monkey jumping on a shivalinga suggests the chaotic, crowded atmosphere at Pashupatinath. It shows disorder, not silence.

questions.q: What does the contrast of the two shrines suggest about Kathmandu?
options: It holds both chaos and calm, varied faiths and moods
questions.why: The contrast between the two shrines suggests that Kathmandu holds both chaos and calm, different faiths and moods. It is not just noisy or just Buddhist.

questions.q: Why does the flute seller's music stand out in the noisy city?
options: Its slow, meditative quality offers a moment of peace amid noise
questions.why: The flute's slow, meditative sound offers a moment of peace amid the city's noise. It stands out by contrast.

courses.title: Ch 9 · If I Were You
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Douglas James's one-act play: an intruder plans to kill Gerrard and take his identity, but quick-witted Gerrard outsmarts him.
outcomes: Learners can retell the plot of the play
Learners can compare Gerrard and the Intruder
Learners can explain presence of mind and dramatic irony
Learners can answer board questions on drama

scenes.text: In a lonely country cottage, a man with a gun surprises Gerrard and announces he will kill him and become him.
Gerrard calmly talks, invents a story, and leads the intruder to a door — which turns out to be a cupboard.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
**Gerrard**, a playwright who lives alone in a remote cottage, is packing a bag when an **Intruder** with a revolver enters. The Intruder is a criminal who has **killed a policeman** and is on the run. He has studied Gerrard — they look alike — and plans to **kill him and take his identity**, living as Gerrard to escape the police.

Gerrard stays calm and witty. He asks questions to learn the Intruder's plan. Then he **bluffs**: he says he himself is a **criminal wanted by the police**, which is why he lives secretly and was about to escape; if the Intruder becomes Gerrard, the police will catch him instead. He even claims a car waits outside to take him away.

The Intruder, alarmed, decides to escape with Gerrard. Gerrard points to a door, saying it leads to the garage. When the Intruder opens it, Gerrard **pushes him into a cupboard** and locks it. Gerrard then phones someone and jokes that he has an 'intruder' for his play — the props were real, suggesting the whole incident gave him material.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body:
- **Gerrard**: a playwright and amateur actor; witty, confident, calm under pressure, sharp-tongued, quick-thinking.
- **Intruder**: a criminal on the run; boastful, careless, overconfident; lacks intelligence; easily fooled.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did the Intruder want to kill Gerrard? (2 marks)** He had killed a policeman and wanted to escape the police by taking Gerrard's identity, as they looked alike and Gerrard lived alone.

**Q2. How did Gerrard trick the Intruder? (3 marks)** He invented a story that he himself was a criminal wanted by the police; this frightened the Intruder; then he led him to a 'garage' door which was actually a cupboard, pushed him in and locked it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The Intruder killed a **policeman**, not a bank guard.
- Gerrard does **not** kill the Intruder; he locks him in a cupboard.

activity.prompt: Order the events of the play
items: Gerrard is packing in his cottage
The Intruder enters with a gun
The Intruder reveals his plan to kill Gerrard and take his identity
Gerrard claims he is a wanted criminal himself
The Intruder decides to escape with him
Gerrard leads him to a 'garage' door and locks him in the cupboard

quiz.why: Gerrard is a playwright, who writes plays. He is not a doctor, thief or policeman.
The Intruder had killed a policeman, and was a dangerous, wanted man. He was hiding from the police.

options: Kill Gerrard and take his identity
quiz.why: The Intruder planned to kill Gerrard and take over his identity, as they looked alike. He wanted to escape that way.

quiz.q: Where did Gerrard lock the Intruder?
quiz.why: Gerrard locked the Intruder in a cupboard at the end. The Intruder had been tricked.
Gerrard bluffed that he was a wanted criminal himself, which frightened the Intruder. The lie was part of his plan.

scenes.text: The Intruder has a gun, but Gerrard has words, wit and calm.
In the end, the man with the weapon ends up locked in a cupboard.

steps.title: Contrast
steps.body:
| Gerrard | Intruder |
- Calm and composed → nervous, boastful
- Witty, uses sarcasm → humourless, slow
- Quick-thinking → careless (believes the bluff)
- Uses intelligence → relies on a gun
- Lives creatively → criminal, violent

steps.title: Drama techniques
steps.body:
- **Dramatic irony**: the audience senses Gerrard is playing a game before the Intruder does.
- **Stage directions** in italics tell actors how to move and speak.
- **Suspense**: will Gerrard survive?
- **Humour**: Gerrard's witty replies lighten the tension.

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. 'Presence of mind can save us in danger.' Discuss with reference to Gerrard. (6 marks)**
Faced with an armed intruder, Gerrard does not panic. He asks questions to understand the plan, stays polite and witty, and studies the Intruder's weaknesses — overconfidence and fear of the police. He then invents a convincing story that he is a wanted criminal, turning the Intruder's plan against him. Finally he tricks him into a cupboard. His calm, quick thinking saves his life, proving that presence of mind can defeat brute force.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Gerrard a coward — he is clever and composed.
- Not citing specific actions as evidence.

activity.prompt: Whose trait is it?

quiz.why: Gerrard's greatest strength is his presence of mind, as he stays calm and thinks quickly. He had no gun or great strength.
The Intruder's weakness is overconfidence, which makes him believe the bluff. He underestimates Gerrard.

quiz.q: Stage directions are usually written in:
quiz.why: Stage directions are usually written in italics or brackets, so they are separate from the dialogue. They guide actors.

options: Audience knows more than a character
quiz.why: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows more than a character does. It adds tension and humour.
'If I Were You' is a one-act play, a short play with a single act. It is not a novel or poem.

scenes.text: A stranger knocks at Tara's home when she is alone and asks to come in to 'check the meter'.
Like Gerrard, she stays calm, keeps the door locked and calls her parents and the society guard.

steps.title: Vocabulary
steps.body:
- **intruder**: a person who enters without permission
- **revolver**: a type of handgun
- **impersonate**: pretend to be another person
- **sinister**: threatening, evil-looking
- **bluff**: deceive by pretending
- **props**: objects used on stage

steps.title: Solved extract (paraphrased)
steps.body:
**Paraphrase:** The Intruder says he has studied Gerrard's habits, knows he lives alone and that few people visit — so no one would notice the switch.
(a) What had the Intruder studied? → Gerrard's habits and life.
(b) Why did Gerrard's lifestyle help the plan? → He lived alone, had few visitors.
(c) Find a word meaning 'pretend to be someone'. → Impersonate (from the chapter's context).

steps.title: Safety lesson
steps.body: If an unknown person tries to enter your home: don't open the door; stay calm; call a parent, a neighbour or **112** (India's emergency number). Never confront an armed person physically.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Intruder' (enters uninvited) vs 'guest'.
- Treating the play's bluffing as advice — in real life, call for help.

a.text: You're home alone. A man at the door says he's from the electricity board and must come in.

choices.label: Open the door — he sounds official
choices.feedback: Never open to strangers when alone; ask for ID through the door and call an adult.

choices.label: Keep the door locked and call a parent or 112
choices.feedback: Correct — stay safe and get help.

b.text: You stop just in time and close the door. What now?

choices.label: Call your parent and the building guard

c.text: Your parent confirms no one was expected. The guard checks and the man leaves. Calm action kept you safe.

quiz.why: An intruder is someone who enters a place without permission. It is not an invited guest.
To impersonate is to pretend to be someone else. The Intruder wanted to impersonate Gerrard.
112 is India's all-in-one emergency number. 911 and 999 are used in other countries.
To bluff is to deceive by pretending, as Gerrard did. It is not telling the truth.

quiz.q: Why did the Intruder think no one would notice?
options: Gerrard lived alone with few visitors
quiz.why: The Intruder thought no one would notice because Gerrard lived alone and had few visitors. This made the swap seem safe.

scenes.text: After locking the Intruder in, Gerrard picks up the phone and laughs.
The audience realises: Gerrard just lived the plot of his next play.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why is the title 'If I Were You' apt? (3 marks)** The Intruder wants to become Gerrard; Gerrard turns this around by saying that if the Intruder became him, the police would catch him as a wanted man. The title captures the theme of switched identities and the danger of wanting to be someone else.

**Q2. What is the significance of the ending? (2 marks)** Gerrard's phone call reveals humour and confidence; the dramatic incident becomes material for his work, showing his wit to the end.

steps.title: Writing link: diary entry as Gerrard
steps.body: Write Gerrard's diary entry that night (100–120 words): what happened, his fear hidden under calm, how he outwitted the Intruder, and his feelings now.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the play is a tragedy — it is a suspenseful comedy-thriller.
- Ignoring the title's double meaning.

steps.title: About the playwright
steps.body: **Douglas James** wrote the one-act play *If I Were You*; it is known for crisp dialogue and suspense.

statements.s: The play has only two main characters.
Gerrard was actually a wanted criminal.
The title refers to the Intruder's wish to become Gerrard.
The Intruder was locked in the garage.

quiz.why: Douglas James wrote the play 'If I Were You'. Shaw, Shakespeare and Chekhov wrote other works.

quiz.q: The genre is best described as:
quiz.why: The play is a suspenseful comedy, a thriller with humour. It is not a tragedy, ballad or epic.
The title is apt because the play is about switching identities, one man planning to be 'you'. It is not a love story or about travel.
A diary entry should include the date and the writer's personal feelings. An address and subject line belong to letters.

options: Makes a phone call, confident and amused
quiz.why: At the end Gerrard makes a phone call, confident and amused, to call the police. He has won by wit.

questions.q: Who is the protagonist?
questions.why: Gerrard is the protagonist, the main character of the play. The Intruder is the antagonist.

questions.q: The Intruder carried a:
questions.why: The Intruder carried a revolver. It is what he used to threaten Gerrard.

questions.q: The setting is:
questions.why: The play is set in a remote cottage, where Gerrard lives alone. This helps the Intruder's plan.

questions.q: Why did the Intruder choose Gerrard?
options: They looked alike and Gerrard lived alone
questions.why: The Intruder chose Gerrard because they looked alike and Gerrard lived alone. It was not a random choice.

questions.q: Gerrard pretended to be:
questions.why: Gerrard pretended to be a wanted criminal, which scared the Intruder. It was a bluff.

questions.q: The Intruder was finally locked in a:
questions.why: The Intruder was finally locked in a cupboard. Gerrard then called the police.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Gerrard survived. Reason (R): He used wit and presence of mind instead of panic.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Gerrard survived because he used wit and presence of mind instead of panicking.

questions.q: Which trait made the Intruder fall for the bluff?
questions.why: The Intruder fell for the bluff because of overconfidence and fear of the police. He was careless.

questions.q: What is the main theme?
options: Presence of mind defeats brute force
questions.why: The main theme is that presence of mind defeats brute force, as wit beats a weapon. It is not about friendship or nature.

questions.q: Stage directions help:
options: Actors know how to act and speak
questions.why: Stage directions guide actors on how to act and speak, and what to do. They are not for readers to skip.

questions.q: Which sequence is correct?
options: Intruder enters → plan revealed → bluff → cupboard
questions.why: The Intruder enters, his plan is revealed, Gerrard bluffs him and locks him in the cupboard. That is the order of the plot.

questions.q: Case: A student says Gerrard should have fought the Intruder physically. Best response from the play:
options: Gerrard's calm wit was safer than fighting an armed man
questions.why: Gerrard's calm wit was safer than fighting an armed man. Fighting a man with a revolver would have been dangerous.

questions.q: What does Gerrard's sarcasm show?
options: Confidence and control of the situation
questions.why: Gerrard's sarcasm shows his confidence and control of the situation. It is not rudeness or fear.

questions.q: Why is the Intruder's plan flawed?
options: He didn't know Gerrard's full life and assumed too much
questions.why: The Intruder's plan was flawed because he did not know Gerrard's full life and assumed too much. He was careless in research.

questions.q: Which is an example of dramatic irony in the play?
options: The audience suspects Gerrard is bluffing while the Intruder believes him
questions.why: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience suspects Gerrard is bluffing while the Intruder believes him. The audience knows more than the Intruder.

courses.title: Beehive Poetry · All poems
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition; the poems in your book may vary — check your syllabus
courses.summary: One lesson per poem: The Road Not Taken, Wind, Rain on the Roof, The Lake Isle of Innisfree, A Legend of the Northland, No Men Are Foreign, On Killing a Tree and A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal — meaning, devices and solved answers.
outcomes: Learners can explain the central idea of each poem
Learners can identify poetic devices (metaphor, alliteration, repetition, imagery, rhyme scheme)
Learners can answer extract-based and long questions on poems
Learners can compare poems by theme

lessons.title: The Road Not Taken — Robert Frost

scenes.text: After Class 10, Dev must choose a stream. Most friends choose science; he loves history.
He remembers Frost's poem: every choice shapes the journey that follows.

steps.title: Meaning (in our own words)
steps.body:
A traveller stands where a road splits into two in a **yellow** (autumn) wood. He wishes he could take both, but he can't. He looks down one as far as he can see, then takes the other, which seemed **grassier and less worn** — though in truth both were about equally worn and covered with fresh leaves. He keeps the first road 'for another day', knowing he will probably never return, because one path leads on to another. He imagines that years later he will tell this story **with a sigh**, saying he chose the road less travelled and that choice **made all the difference**.

**Central idea**: life is full of choices; we cannot take every path; our choices shape our lives, and we often look back on them with mixed feelings.

steps.title: Poetic devices
steps.body:
- **Metaphor**: the roads = choices in life; the wood = life's journey.
- **Imagery**: yellow wood (autumn), leaves no step had trodden black.
- **Rhyme scheme**: **ABAAB** in each of four five-line stanzas.
- **Repetition**: 'two roads diverged'.
- **Inversion**: word order changed for rhyme (e.g., 'And looked down one as far as I could').

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did the poet choose the second road? (2 marks)** It seemed grassier and less used, so it 'wanted wear' — though actually both were similar.

**Q2. Why will he tell the story 'with a sigh'? (2 marks)** The sigh could mean regret or satisfaction — he can never know how the other road would have turned out.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The poem doesn't simply say 'be different' — it notes both roads were really about the same.
- Rhyme scheme is **ABAAB**, not ABAB.

statements.s: Both roads were really about equally worn.
The poet took both roads.
The rhyme scheme is ABAAB.
The 'yellow wood' suggests autumn.

quiz.why: The two roads stand for the choices we make in life. They are not real highways.
The rhyme scheme of 'The Road Not Taken' is ABAAB in each stanza. This is Frost's pattern.

quiz.q: The poet kept the first road for:
quiz.why: The poet kept the first road for another day, though he doubted that he would ever return. It shows how choices close other doors.
The season is autumn, as shown by the yellow wood and fallen leaves. It is not spring or summer.
Robert Frost wrote 'The Road Not Taken'. Kirkup, Yeats and Wordsworth wrote other poems.

scenes.text: A storm tears off the loose tin roof of a weak shed, but a sturdy house nearby stands firm.
The poem's message: make yourself strong, and the wind becomes your friend.

steps.title: Meaning (in our own words)
steps.body:
The poet speaks to the wind: don't break the window shutters, don't scatter the papers, don't throw down the books on the shelf. But the wind has already done so — torn pages, broken things — and even hurt the frail. The wind **winnows** (separates) the weak: crumbling houses, doors, rafters, wood, bodies, lives and hearts — it **crushes them all**. So the poet advises: **build strong homes, join the doors firmly, practise to firm the body, make the heart steadfast**. The wind won't be able to harm the strong; it **befriends** them. The fire burning low, the wind blows it out; strong fires roar and flourish with the wind. 'We praise him every day' — the wind (a symbol of hardships) is to be respected.

**Central idea**: hardships (wind) destroy the weak but make the strong stronger; so we must build inner strength.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Personification**: wind breaks, scatters, pours rain, winnows.
- **Symbolism**: wind = difficulties of life.
- **Free verse**: no regular rhyme.
- **Repetition**: 'crumbling'.
- **Translated** from Tamil (poet Subramania Bharati).

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What does the wind do to weak things? (2 marks)** It breaks, scatters and crushes them — weak houses, doors, rafters, bodies and hearts.

**Q2. How can we make friends with the wind? (2 marks)** By building strong homes, strong bodies and steadfast hearts — being strong in face of difficulties.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The poem is not about weather alone — the wind is a **symbol**.
- 'Winnow' means separate grain from chaff — here, separate the weak from the strong.

activity.prompt: Match the image to its meaning
pairs: A strong person grows with challenges
Separate the weak from the strong

quiz.why: In 'Wind', the wind symbolises hardships and difficulties in life. It is not wealth or happiness.
The wind befriends the strong, as it only harms the weak. The poet says we should be strong to face it.
The poem 'Wind' is translated from Tamil, written by Subramania Bharati. It was not translated from Hindi or Bengali.
'Winnow' means to separate grain from chaff. Here the wind does this to strong people's weaknesses.
The main device is personification, as the wind acts like a person who breaks and attacks. It is not a pun.

lessons.title: Rain on the Roof — Coates Kinney

scenes.text: Rain patters on the tin roof of Grandma's house. Rehan lies in bed listening.
He suddenly remembers his mother tucking him in years ago. The sound brings memories flooding back.

steps.title: Meaning (in our own words)
steps.body:
When dark clouds gather and the night is humid, the poet loves to lie in his cottage bed and listen to the **patter of soft rain** on the shingles (roof). Each sound **echoes in his heart**; a thousand dreamy fancies come into his mind. In this mood, memories return — especially of his **mother**, as she used to look at him lovingly before he fell asleep, years ago. Her loving look returns to him as he listens to the rain on the roof.

**Central idea**: nature (rain) awakens happy childhood memories and love for the mother.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Alliteration**: 'humid shadows hover', 'patter of the soft rain'.
- **Imagery**: dark clouds, shingles, cottage bed.
- **Onomatopoeia**: patter.
- **Metaphor/personification**: memories 'weave' their air-threads into woof.
- **Rhyme scheme**: ABCB (in each stanza, lines 2 and 4 rhyme).

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What does the poet like to do when it rains? (2 marks)** Lie in his cottage bed and listen to the patter of the soft rain overhead.

**Q2. Whom does the poet remember? (2 marks)** His mother, who lovingly looked at him as a child when he went to bed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The poet's mother is not present — he **remembers** her.
- Shingles are roof tiles, not stones on a beach.

activity.prompt: Complete the summary
activity.text: The poet listens to the ___ of the rain on the roof and remembers his ___.

quiz.why: The poet lies in his cottage bed, listening to the rain on the roof. The setting is cosy.
He remembers his mother, who used to sing to him. The rain on the roof brings back memories.
'Patter' imitates a sound, so it is onomatopoeia. It is not a simile or pun.
Shingles are roof tiles, or roof coverings. They are not leaves or pebbles.
The mood of the poem is nostalgic and tender, full of memories of his mother. It is not fearful or angry.

lessons.title: The Lake Isle of Innisfree — W.B. Yeats

scenes.text: In a noisy city traffic jam, Meera closes her eyes and pictures her grandmother's village pond.
Like Yeats, she hears the water in her heart, even on grey pavements.

steps.title: Meaning (in our own words)
steps.body:
The poet longs to go to **Innisfree**, a small island in a lake in Ireland. There he will build a **small cabin of clay and wattles**, have **nine bean-rows** and a **hive for the honey-bee**, and live alone in a glade loud with bees.

He will find **peace** there, which comes dropping slowly: morning veils, crickets singing; midnight 'all a glimmer'; noon a purple glow (heather); evening full of linnets' wings.

He will go, because always — night and day — he hears lake water lapping with low sounds by the shore. Even while he stands on the **roadway or on grey pavements** (in the city), he hears it **in the deep heart's core**.

**Central idea**: longing for the peace of nature and a simple life, away from the city.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Imagery**: bean-rows, bee-loud glade, purple glow, linnets' wings.
- **Alliteration**: 'lake water lapping with low sounds'.
- **Contrast**: grey pavements (city) vs the island (nature).
- **Rhyme scheme**: **ABAB**.
- **Metaphor**: peace 'comes dropping slow'.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What kind of place is Innisfree? (2 marks)** A quiet lake island in Ireland, full of natural beauty, where the poet can live simply and peacefully.

**Q2. What does 'in the deep heart's core' mean? (2 marks)** He feels the call of the lake deep within his heart, even in the city.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Innisfree is in **Ireland**, not England.
- He wants **nine** bean-rows (not ten).

activity.prompt: City or Innisfree?

quiz.why: Innisfree is a small island in a lake in Ireland. The poet Yeats longed to go there.

quiz.q: How many bean-rows does he want?
quiz.why: He wants nine bean-rows on Innisfree. The number is nine in the poem.

quiz.q: His cabin will be made of:
quiz.why: His cabin will be made of clay and wattles, a simple natural structure. It is not made of glass or stone.
The rhyme scheme of 'The Lake Isle of Innisfree' is ABAB in each stanza. ABAAB belongs to Frost's poem.

quiz.q: Where does he hear the lake water?
options: On the pavements, in his heart's core
quiz.why: The poet hears the lake water on the pavements, in the city, deep in his heart's core. He carries the memory with him.

lessons.title: A Legend of the Northland — Phoebe Cary

scenes.text: A hungry traveller asks a woman for one cake. She keeps baking smaller ones — but finds each too big to give away.
Angered, the traveller turns her into a bird who must bore into wood for food.

steps.title: Meaning (in our own words)
steps.body:
This is a **ballad** — a story-poem — set in the **Northland**, where days are short and nights long and people ride in sledges with reindeer. Children are told a legend there.

**Saint Peter**, wandering the world, comes to a cottage where a little woman is baking cakes. Tired and hungry after fasting all day, he asks for one. She makes a **very small cake**, but it seems too big to give. She makes smaller ones, but each looks too large; finally she puts her wafer-thin piece on the shelf, refusing to give anything.

St Peter, angry, says she is too selfish to dwell in human form — he turns her into a **woodpecker**, who will have to bore into hard, dry wood all day for scanty food. She flies up the chimney as a bird with a **red cap** (her scarlet cap) and a **coal-black** body (her dress burnt black). Every schoolboy may still see her in the woods, boring and boring for food.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Ballad**: a narrative poem, often of folk origin, in short stanzas.
- **Rhyme scheme**: ABCB.
- **Simile**: 'she was too selfish'… and comparisons of cakes becoming smaller.
- **Moral**: greed and selfishness are punished; kindness is a virtue.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did St Peter punish the woman? (2 marks)** She was too greedy and selfish to give even a tiny cake to a hungry, tired man.

**Q2. How does the woodpecker remind us of the woman? (2 marks)** Its red cap and black body recall her scarlet cap and dress blackened by soot; and it must work hard for scanty food.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- She was changed into a **woodpecker**, not a crow.
- The visitor is **Saint Peter**.

activity.prompt: Order the events of the ballad
items: St Peter arrives hungry at a cottage
He asks the woman for a cake
She bakes smaller and smaller cakes but gives none
St Peter angrily curses her
She turns into a woodpecker and flies up the chimney
She must bore into wood for food

quiz.why: 'A Legend of the Northland' is a ballad, a poem that tells a story. It is not a sonnet or haiku.

quiz.q: The woman was turned into a:
quiz.why: The greedy woman was turned into a woodpecker, as punishment for her greed. She was not changed into a sparrow or crow.
Saint Peter asked the woman for a cake. He had come in disguise to test her.
The woodpecker has a red cap on its head. It is the mark of the old woman.
The moral is against greed and selfishness. Kindness is the quality that the poem praises.

lessons.title: No Men Are Foreign — James Kirkup

scenes.text: Ayesha writes to a pen-friend in another country. They discover they both love mangoes, cricket and their grandmothers.
'No men are foreign,' her teacher says. 'We share one earth.'

steps.title: Meaning (in our own words)
steps.body:
The poet says that **no person is foreign** and no country strange. Beneath all uniforms, a single body breathes like ours; we walk on the same land and will be buried in it. People everywhere are aware of **sun, air and water**, are fed by **peaceful harvests** and starved by war's long winter. Their hands, like ours, show labour; their eyes, like ours, wake and sleep, and can be won by love.

So we should **remember** that whenever we are told to hate our brothers, it is **ourselves** we betray and condemn. When we take up arms against others, we **pollute and destroy the earth** that we all share. 'Hells of fire and dust' from war outrage the innocence of air, which is everywhere our own.

**Central idea**: universal brotherhood; war harms everyone, including ourselves.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Repetition**: 'Remember', 'like ours'.
- **Metaphor**: 'war's long winter' (war = harsh winter of hunger).
- **Imagery**: peaceful harvests; hells of fire and dust.
- **Free verse** with a sense of rhythm.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Name three things all people share. (2 marks)** The same earth, sun, air and water; similar bodies, labour and feelings.

**Q2. How do we 'defile' the earth? (2 marks)** By war — weapons, fire and dust pollute and destroy the shared earth and air.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Uniforms' here means **any outward differences** (clothes, nationality), not only army dress.
- The poem opposes **war**, not patriotism itself.

statements.s: The poet says some countries are strange.
War's long winter is a metaphor.
Hating others means betraying ourselves.
The poem praises war.

quiz.why: The central theme of 'No Men Are Foreign' is universal brotherhood: all people are alike. It is not childhood or patriotism.
'War's long winter' compares war to a winter without directly using 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor. A simile uses 'like' or 'as'.

quiz.q: The word repeated for emphasis is:
quiz.why: The word 'remember' is repeated for emphasis, to remind us that all people are alike. Repetition stresses the message.
James Kirkup wrote 'No Men Are Foreign'. Frost and Yeats wrote other poems.
The poem says that taking up arms against others defiles our shared earth. It harms the common earth, so it does not protect it.

lessons.title: On Killing a Tree — Gieve Patel

scenes.text: Workers chop an old tree near the school. A month later, green shoots appear from the stump.
The students realise: a tree is not easy to kill. Nature fights to live.

steps.title: Meaning (in our own words)
steps.body:
The poet says it takes much time to kill a tree — **not a simple jab of the knife**. A tree grows slowly, consuming the earth, absorbing sunlight, air and water for years, and leprous hide (bark) grows over it. If you just hack and chop it, the bleeding bark will heal and green twigs will grow again from close to the ground — curled sprigs that will become boughs. 

To truly kill it, the **root must be pulled out** of the earth — the strength of the tree, hidden for years in the earth. Then its white, wet, most sensitive part is exposed; it must be left to **scorch and choke in sun and air** — browning, hardening, twisting, withering — until it is done.

**Central idea**: through **irony**, the poet condemns cutting trees and shows the tree's strong will to live; human cruelty to nature.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Irony**: instructions on how to kill a tree actually protest against it.
- **Personification**: tree 'bleeds', has 'hide'.
- **Imagery**: 'leprous hide', 'bleeding bark'.
- **Alliteration**: 'bleeding bark', 'sprouting… sprigs'.
- **Free verse**; final line lists verbs: browning, hardening, twisting, withering.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why isn't a simple jab of the knife enough? (2 marks)** The tree's bark heals and new twigs sprout from near the ground; its root remains strong.

**Q2. What is the final step in killing a tree? (2 marks)** Pull out the root, expose it to the sun and air, and let it scorch, choke, brown, harden, twist and wither.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The poem is **ironic** — it does not actually recommend killing trees.
- The 'anchoring earth' holds the roots.

activity.prompt: Order the steps the poem describes (ironically)
items: Hacking and chopping the trunk is not enough
The bark heals and new twigs sprout
The root must be pulled out of the earth
The root is exposed to sun and air
It scorches and chokes
It browns, hardens, twists and withers

quiz.q: The main device of the poem is:
quiz.why: The main device of 'On Killing a Tree' is irony, as the poet seems to describe how to kill a tree, but protests against it. It is not just alliteration.

quiz.q: The tree's real strength lies in its:
quiz.why: The tree's real strength lies in its root, deep in the earth. Cutting the trunk is not enough to kill it.
'Bleeding bark' gives a human quality to the tree, so it is personification. It is not onomatopoeia or a simile.
Gieve Patel wrote 'On Killing a Tree'. Kinney and Kirkup wrote other poems.

options: Human cruelty to nature and the tree's will to live
quiz.why: The poem is about human cruelty to nature and the tree's will to live. It is not about gardening or carpentry.

lessons.title: A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal — William Wordsworth

scenes.text: After his grandfather passes away, Aryan feels he never imagined it could happen.
His teacher reads him Wordsworth's short poem about loss and nature's endless cycle.

steps.title: Meaning (in our own words)
steps.body:
This short poem (two four-line stanzas) is one of Wordsworth's 'Lucy' poems. In the first stanza, the poet says a kind of **sleep (slumber) sealed his spirit** — he was unaware; he had no human fears; she seemed a thing that could not feel the touch of earthly years (he thought she would never age or die).

In the second stanza, she has **died**: she has no motion and no force now; she neither hears nor sees; she is rolled round in earth's **daily (diurnal) course** with **rocks, stones and trees** — she has become part of nature.

**Central idea**: the shock of a loved one's death; death as a return to nature.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **Contrast** between the two stanzas: illusion of immortality vs the reality of death.
- **Metaphor**: 'slumber' = unawareness.
- **Imagery**: rocks, stones and trees.
- **Rhyme scheme**: ABAB.
- 'Diurnal' = daily (earth's rotation).

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. What 'slumber' sealed the poet's spirit? (2 marks)** A state of unawareness in which he never imagined his loved one could age or die.

**Q2. How is she now part of nature? (2 marks)** After death she is still, without senses, rolled round with the earth's daily motion along with rocks, stones and trees.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The poem is about **death**, not sleep literally.
- 'Diurnal' means **daily**, not nightly.

steps.title: On grief
steps.body: Grief is natural. Talking to family, a teacher or a counsellor helps. In India, the **Tele-MANAS** helpline (**14416**) offers free mental-health support.

activity.prompt: Match the words
pairs: Nature she has become part of

quiz.why: 'Diurnal' means daily, relating to the day. In the poem it describes the earth's daily rotation.
'A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal' deals with the death of a loved one. The poet tells of her passing.
The poem has two stanzas, each of four lines (quatrains). It is not one or four.
William Wordsworth wrote 'A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal'. Frost and Yeats wrote other poems.
The rhyme scheme of the poem is ABAB in each stanza. ABAAB belongs to 'The Road Not Taken'.

questions.q: Who wrote 'The Road Not Taken'?
questions.why: Robert Frost wrote 'The Road Not Taken'. Kirkup, Yeats and Wordsworth wrote other poems.

questions.q: Which poem is a ballad?
questions.why: 'A Legend of the Northland' is a ballad, a story told in verse. The other poems do not tell a story.

questions.q: Innisfree is a:
questions.why: Innisfree is a small island in a lake, in Ireland. It is not a mountain, desert or city.

questions.q: In 'Wind', the wind befriends:
questions.why: In 'Wind' the wind befriends the strong, and attacks the weak. This is the poem's message.

questions.q: In 'Rain on the Roof', the poet remembers his:
questions.why: In 'Rain on the Roof' the poet remembers his mother, as the rain brings back memories. The poem is tender.

questions.q: The woman in the ballad became a:
questions.why: The greedy old woman in the ballad was changed into a woodpecker. It was her punishment.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 'On Killing a Tree' is ironic. Reason (R): It describes how to kill a tree to protest against tree-cutting.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The poem seems to explain how to kill a tree, but this is a protest against tree-cutting, which is irony.

questions.q: Which line of thought belongs to 'No Men Are Foreign'?
questions.why: 'No Men Are Foreign' says that hating others betrays ourselves, as all men are alike. The other lines belong to other poems.

questions.q: Rhyme scheme ABAAB belongs to:
options: A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal
questions.why: The rhyme scheme ABAAB belongs to Frost's 'The Road Not Taken'. The other poems use different patterns.

questions.q: 'Lake water lapping with low sounds' shows:
questions.why: 'Lake water lapping with low sounds' repeats the 'l' sound, which is alliteration. It is not a pun or oxymoron.

questions.q: Which two poems contrast city life/war with peaceful nature?
options: Innisfree and No Men Are Foreign
Wind and Rain on the Roof
questions.why: Innisfree contrasts city life with peaceful nature, and 'No Men Are Foreign' contrasts war with peace and unity. So these two fit the pair.

questions.q: Case: A builder says trees can be cut and will regrow anyway. Which poem would a student quote to show it takes much to kill a tree, and why it shouldn't be done?
questions.why: 'On Killing a Tree' shows how much effort it takes to kill a tree, and protests against such cruelty. The builder's claim would be answered by it.

questions.q: In 'A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal', the two stanzas contrast:
options: Illusion of immortality and the reality of death
