questions.why: In 'A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal', the first stanza shows the illusion of immortality, and the second the reality of death. It does not contrast city and village.

questions.q: The 'sigh' in 'The Road Not Taken' suggests:
options: Mixed feelings — regret or satisfaction — about choices
questions.why: The 'sigh' shows mixed feelings, either regret or satisfaction, about the choice made. The poet's meaning is ambiguous.

questions.q: Which poem's message is 'strength of mind and body helps us face hardships'?
questions.why: 'Wind' by Subramania Bharati says that strength of mind and body helps us face hardships. The other poems have other messages.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Coates Kinney – On Killing a Tree
questions.why: Subramania Bharati wrote 'Wind', translated from Tamil, so that pair is correct. Innisfree was by Yeats, 'On Killing a Tree' by Gieve Patel, and 'Rain on the Roof' by Kinney.

school-c9-english-c.title: Class 9 English · Moments & Grammar I
school-c9-english-c.description: The Class 9 supplementary reader Moments — one lesson per story — plus grammar courses on tenses, modals and determiners with solved examples, editing practice and tests.

courses.title: Moments · Supplementary Reader (all stories)
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition; the stories in your book may vary — check your syllabus
courses.summary: Eight stories from Moments: The Lost Child, The Adventures of Toto, Iswaran the Storyteller, In the Kingdom of Fools, The Happy Prince, The Last Leaf, A House Is Not a Home and The Beggar — summaries in original words, characters, themes and solved long answers.
outcomes: Learners can summarise each story
Learners can write character sketches with evidence
Learners can explain the theme and message of each story
Learners can answer 6-mark value-based questions

lessons.title: The Lost Child — Mulk Raj Anand

scenes.text: At a crowded fair, little Chintu lets go of his mother's hand to watch a merry-go-round.
When he turns around, she's gone. Nothing at the fair matters any more — he only wants his parents.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
On a spring festival day, a little boy walks to the fair with his parents. On the way and at the fair he wants everything: **toys**, **sweets (burfi)**, a **garland of gulmohur flowers**, **balloons**, to watch a **snake-charmer** and to ride the **roundabout**. Each time his parents refuse or he knows they will, and he moves on.

When he finally asks to ride the roundabout, he finds his parents **missing**. Terrified, he runs about crying for his mother and father. A kind man lifts him up and tries to comfort him by offering the very things he had wanted — a ride, balloons, flowers, sweets. But the child **refuses everything**, sobbing that he wants his mother and father.

**Theme**: a child's deepest need is the love and security of parents; material things lose meaning without them.

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. Why did the child refuse the things he had wanted earlier? (6 marks)**
At the fair the child longed for toys, sweets, a garland, balloons and a ride, but his parents denied him. Once he lost them, fear and loneliness filled him. The kind stranger offered all those things, yet the child refused, crying for his parents. This shows that his desires were only small pleasures when he felt safe; real happiness for a child lies in the security and love of his parents. Without them, nothing else matters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The festival is in **spring**, not winter.
- The stranger is **kind**, not a kidnapper.

steps.title: Safety tip
steps.body: If you get lost in a crowd: stay where you are, look for a police officer, security guard or a family with children, and tell them your parent's phone number. Teach younger siblings their parents' number.

activity.prompt: Order the child's wishes and the climax
items: He wants toys at the shop
He wants burfi from the sweet-seller
He wants a garland of gulmohur
He wants balloons
He watches a snake-charmer
He wants to ride the roundabout and finds his parents gone
He refuses everything the stranger offers

quiz.why: The festival in 'The Lost Child' was a spring festival. It is the setting of the story.
The boy wanted to buy burfi, a sweet. He first wanted toys and then sweets.

quiz.q: What did he want to ride?
quiz.why: The boy wanted to ride on the roundabout at the fair. He soon forgot it when he lost his parents.

quiz.q: Why did he refuse the stranger's offers?
quiz.why: He refused the stranger's offers because he only wanted his parents. All sweets and toys seemed worthless to him.
Mulk Raj Anand wrote 'The Lost Child'. Ruskin Bond and R.K. Narayan wrote other stories.

lessons.title: The Adventures of Toto — Ruskin Bond

scenes.text: Grandfather brings home a red monkey with bright eyes and mischief in his heart.
Within days, wallpaper is torn, clothes ripped and dishes broken. The family's patience runs out.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
The narrator's **Grandfather**, who kept a private zoo, bought a monkey named **Toto** from a **tonga-driver** for **five rupees**. Toto was pretty, with bright eyes and a long tail he used like a hand. To hide him from Grandmother, he was kept in a **cupboard** in the narrator's room, tied to a peg — but Toto pulled out the peg and tore the wallpaper and the narrator's school blazer.

Then Grandfather put Toto in the **servants' quarters** with other pets — but Toto troubled them all. When Grandfather went to **Saharanpur** by train to collect his pension, he took Toto in a black bag; the **ticket-collector** insisted Toto be charged as a dog, and Grandfather had to pay a fare.

Toto once nearly **boiled himself alive** in a large kettle of warm water put on the fire — he liked hot baths. He broke dishes, tore clothes, and ate Grandmother's food. Finally the family realised Toto could not be kept, and Grandfather **sold him back to the tonga-driver for three rupees**.

steps.title: Humour and character
steps.body:
- Toto is **mischievous**, intelligent and destructive — the humour comes from his antics.
- Grandfather is kind and fond of animals, but finally gives up.
- The narrator tells the story with gentle humour and nostalgia.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did Grandfather sell Toto? (2 marks)** Toto was too destructive and costly to keep — tearing clothes and wallpaper, breaking dishes — and the family could not afford his mischief.

**Q2. Why was Toto charged as a dog on the train? (2 marks)** The ticket-collector insisted any animal in a bag had to be paid for like a dog.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Bought for **five** rupees, sold for **three**.
- Grandfather went to **Saharanpur**, not Dehradun.

statements.s: Toto was bought for five rupees.
Toto was sold for ten rupees.
Toto nearly boiled himself in a kettle.
Grandfather took Toto to Saharanpur in a bag.

quiz.why: Toto was a pet monkey, bought by Grandfather. He was very mischievous.
Grandfather bought Toto from a tonga-driver, who had him in his possession. He was a young monkey.

quiz.q: Where did Grandfather go by train?
quiz.why: Grandfather went to Saharanpur by train, taking Toto with him. Toto caused trouble on the way.
Toto was sold back for three rupees, at a loss to Grandfather. He had been bought for more.
Ruskin Bond wrote 'The Adventures of Toto'. O. Henry and Chekhov wrote other stories.

story.title: A cook with a thousand tales

scenes.text: In a lonely work camp, Mahendra's cook Iswaran makes delicious food from almost nothing — and tells thrilling stories every night.
One night, after a ghost story, Mahendra sees a strange figure in the moonlight — and decides to leave.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
**Mahendra**, a junior supervisor in a firm, is moved from one work site to another — building sites, bridges, factories — often in remote places. His cook **Iswaran** follows him everywhere. Iswaran is resourceful, cheerful, and a gifted **storyteller**: he can turn the smallest incident into an exciting tale, with suspense and drama.

One story describes how, as a boy, he faced a **wild tusker** that had escaped into a timber yard and caused panic; Iswaran claims he subdued it with a stick blow to its toe — Mahendra wonders if it is true. Iswaran's stories of **ghosts** fascinate and frighten Mahendra.

When the site is near an old **burial ground**, Iswaran tells of a **female ghost** with a dishevelled look who appears on **full-moon nights**. Mahendra laughs, but one night he wakes, hears a moan and sees a dark, cloudy figure near his window. Shaken, he decides to **leave the haunted place** the next day.

steps.title: Characters and theme
steps.body:
- **Iswaran**: resourceful, cheerful, imaginative, a natural storyteller; uses suspense and exaggeration.
- **Mahendra**: practical, simple; claims not to believe in ghosts but is influenced by stories.
- **Theme**: the power of storytelling and imagination over the human mind.

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. How did Iswaran's storytelling affect Mahendra? (6 marks)**
Iswaran's tales were vivid and full of suspense, using dramatic pauses and exaggeration. Mahendra enjoyed them as entertainment in his lonely camps. Though practical, he was gradually influenced. When Iswaran described the female ghost seen on full-moon nights near the burial ground, Mahendra laughed at first. But on a full-moon night he heard moaning and saw a shadowy figure, and the fear Iswaran had planted took over. He decided to leave. This shows how powerful imagination and storytelling can be.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mahendra was a **junior supervisor**, not a factory owner.
- The ghost is described as **female**, seen on **full-moon** nights.

activity.prompt: Match the detail
pairs: Junior supervisor moved from site to site
Iswaran claims he subdued a wild elephant
When the ghost was said to appear

quiz.why: Mahendra worked as a junior supervisor on a construction site. Iswaran was his cook.
Iswaran was Mahendra's cook. He was also a great storyteller.
Iswaran's special talent was storytelling, and he told wonderful tales. He was not known for painting or dancing.

quiz.q: Why did Mahendra leave the site?
options: He was frightened by the ghost
quiz.why: Mahendra left the site because the ghost story frightened him, as it came true. He was terrified by it.
As given in the textbook, 'Iswaran the Storyteller' is credited to R.K. Laxman. Mulk Raj Anand and Ruskin Bond wrote other stories.

lessons.title: In the Kingdom of Fools — folktale retold by A.K. Ramanujan

scenes.text: Two travellers reach a kingdom where everything — rice, bananas, sweets — costs one coin.
The wise guru says, 'Let's leave; fools rule here.' The greedy disciple stays for cheap food — and nearly loses his life.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
In a kingdom ruled by a foolish **king** and his **minister**, people must work at **night** and sleep by day. A **guru** and his **disciple** arrive and find everything costs **one duddu** (coin). The guru, seeing the foolishness, decides to leave; the disciple stays for the cheap food and grows fat.

One night a **thief** breaks into a merchant's house; the old **wall collapses** and kills him. The thief's brother complains to the king. In a chain of blame, the king blames the **merchant**, who blames the **bricklayer**, who blames a **dancing girl** (distracting him), who blames the **goldsmith** (who delayed her jewellery), who says the merchant had ordered jewellery first. The king orders the merchant to be **impaled** — but he is too thin; the king orders a **fat man** found to be executed instead. The fat disciple is caught.

The disciple prays to his guru. The guru arrives and whispers a plan; both begin quarrelling, each wanting to die first. Asked why, the guru says that whoever dies on this stake at this moment will be **reborn as king**, and the next as minister. The king and minister, wanting to rule again, have themselves executed secretly. The people then make the guru and disciple king and minister; the guru changes the foolish laws.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- Foolish rule brings injustice.
- **Wisdom vs greed**: the guru's wisdom saves the disciple; greed nearly kills him.
- Listen to wise advice.
- Folk humour and satire on irrational authority.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why did the guru want to leave the kingdom? (2 marks)** He realised that a kingdom where everything costs the same and laws are absurd is ruled by fools, and life there could be unpredictable and dangerous.

**Q2. How did the guru save the disciple? (3 marks)** He convinced the king that whoever died on the stake first would be reborn as king; the foolish king and minister chose to die themselves, freeing the disciple.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The coin is a **duddu**.
- The disciple was chosen because he was **fat** enough for the stake.

activity.prompt: Order the chain of blame
items: The thief's brother complains to the king
The king blames the merchant
The merchant blames the bricklayer
The bricklayer blames the dancing girl
The dancing girl blames the goldsmith
The goldsmith blames the merchant's order
The king sentences the merchant, then a fat man

quiz.q: In the kingdom of fools, everything cost:
quiz.why: In the kingdom of fools, everything cost one duddu, whether it was vegetables or sweets. This shows the foolishness of the place.
In the kingdom of fools, people worked at night and slept by day. Their ways were upside down.

quiz.q: Why was the disciple chosen for execution?
options: He was fat enough for the stake
quiz.why: The disciple was chosen for execution because he was fat enough for the stake. The king's men used foolish logic.

quiz.q: The king and minister died because:
options: They wanted to be reborn as king and minister
quiz.why: The king and the minister died because they wanted to be reborn as king and minister, as the guru tricked them. This was the guru's clever plan.

options: Greed and foolishness lead to danger; wisdom saves
quiz.why: The lesson is that greed and foolishness lead to danger, while wisdom saves. It does not support working at night or buying cheap food.

scenes.text: A golden statue with sapphire eyes looks down on the city and sees poverty everywhere.
He asks a little swallow to give away his jewels and gold, one by one, to those who suffer.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
High above the city stands the statue of the **Happy Prince**, covered in thin leaves of fine **gold**, with **sapphires** for eyes and a **ruby** on his sword-hilt. In life he lived in the palace of Sans-Souci, where sorrow was not allowed, so he was called happy. Now, as a statue, he sees the misery of the city and weeps.

A **swallow**, flying to Egypt for winter, rests at his feet. The Prince asks him to take the **ruby** to a poor **seamstress** whose son lies ill with fever; then a **sapphire** to a young **playwright** too cold and hungry to finish his play; then the other **sapphire** to a little **match girl** whose matches have fallen in the gutter. Now blind, the Prince asks the swallow to stay and peel off the **gold leaf** to give to the poor. The swallow stays, out of love; winter comes, and he **dies of cold** at the Prince's feet. At that moment the Prince's **lead heart cracks**.

The Mayor and Councillors, finding the statue shabby, melt it down; the broken lead heart will not melt and is thrown on a dust heap beside the dead swallow. God asks an angel to bring the two most precious things in the city; the angel brings the **lead heart** and the **dead bird**, and they are rewarded in paradise.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Compassion and sacrifice** — true happiness lies in helping others.
- **Contrast** between outward beauty (gold, jewels) and inner goodness (heart).
- **Social criticism** — the rich ignore the poor; officials value appearance.

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. Why were the lead heart and the dead bird the most precious things in the city? (6 marks)**
The Happy Prince gave away his ruby, sapphires and gold to relieve the suffering of the seamstress, the playwright, the match girl and the poor. The swallow gave up his journey to Egypt and his life to help the Prince. Their acts of love and sacrifice made them truly valuable, though the city saw them as worthless — a broken heart and a dead bird. God valued their goodness over gold, showing that compassion is more precious than wealth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The ruby went to the **seamstress**; sapphires to the **playwright** and the **match girl**.
- The swallow was going to **Egypt**.

activity.prompt: Who received which gift?
pairs: The seamstress with a sick son

quiz.why: The Happy Prince's statue had sapphires for eyes. A sapphire is a blue gem.
The swallow was going to Egypt for the winter. He stayed on to help the Prince.
The Prince's ruby, from his sword hilt, went to a seamstress for her sick child. The swallow carried it.

quiz.q: What didn't melt in the furnace?
quiz.why: The lead heart did not melt in the furnace, as it had broken when the swallow died. It was kept as the most precious thing.

quiz.q: The two most precious things were:
quiz.why: The two most precious things in the city were the lead heart and the dead bird, which showed love and sacrifice. The angel chose them.

scenes.text: Sick with pneumonia, Johnsy stares at an ivy vine outside her window, counting the falling leaves.
'When the last one falls, I'll die,' she says. That night, through a storm, someone makes sure one leaf never falls.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
**Sue** and **Johnsy**, two young artists, share a small apartment. Johnsy falls ill with **pneumonia** and loses the will to live. The **doctor** tells Sue that Johnsy's chances are slim unless she wants to live.

Johnsy watches an old **ivy vine** on the wall opposite and counts its leaves as they fall, believing she will **die when the last leaf falls**. Sue tells their downstairs neighbour, **Behrman**, an old, unsuccessful painter who always talks of painting a masterpiece.

That night a fierce storm rages. In the morning, one leaf still clings to the vine — and the next day too. Johnsy feels ashamed of wanting to die, regains hope, and begins to recover. Later, Sue learns that Behrman died of **pneumonia** after spending the stormy night outside, painting a leaf on the wall where the last one had fallen. The leaf was his **masterpiece**.

steps.title: Themes and technique
steps.body:
- **Hope and the will to live**.
- **Sacrifice and friendship**: Behrman gives his life; Sue cares devotedly.
- **Art's power**: Behrman's true masterpiece saved a life.
- O. Henry's trademark **twist ending**.

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. Why is the leaf called Behrman's masterpiece? (6 marks)**
Behrman, a failed old artist, always dreamed of painting a masterpiece. When Johnsy lost the will to live and believed she would die with the last ivy leaf, Behrman painted a leaf on the wall during a stormy night. It looked so real that Johnsy believed it had survived the storm, regained hope and recovered. Behrman caught pneumonia and died. The leaf was a masterpiece not for its fame but because it saved a life through art and sacrifice.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- It was **Johnsy** who was ill, not Sue.
- The vine was an **ivy**, not a mango tree.

statements.s: Johnsy had pneumonia.
statements.why: She lost the will to live.

statements.s: Behrman was a successful, famous artist.
statements.why: He was an unsuccessful old painter.

statements.s: The last leaf was painted on the wall.
Behrman died of pneumonia.
statements.why: He caught it in the storm.

quiz.q: Johnsy believed she would die when:
quiz.why: Johnsy believed she would die when the last leaf fell from the ivy vine. She had lost her will to live.
Behrman, an old painter, painted the last leaf on the wall. It saved Johnsy's life.
The vine on the wall was an ivy. Johnsy counted its falling leaves.
The ending is a twist, as the last leaf was painted by Behrman, who died of pneumonia. This is O. Henry's style.
The main theme is hope and sacrifice, as Behrman gives his life to save Johnsy. It is not about revenge or greed.

lessons.title: A House Is Not a Home — Zan Gaudioso

scenes.text: A teenager, already struggling at a new high school, watches his family's house burn down.
Days later, classmates he barely knew arrive with bags of clothes, books and supplies. He finally feels he belongs.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
The narrator, a 14-year-old starting **high school**, misses his old school and friends and feels alone in the new place. He also still grieves for his **grandmother**, who had died earlier.

One evening the family's **house catches fire**. They escape, but their belongings — memories, photos, everything — are lost. He is also devastated because his beloved **cat** seems to be lost in the confusion.

While living with relatives, he goes to school with nothing. To his surprise, students and teachers — many he hardly knew — come forward with **school supplies, clothes, books and gifts**. Their kindness overwhelms him; he realises that his community cares. Later, the **cat is found and returned** to him, which brings great relief.

**Theme**: a 'home' is not just a building but the love of family and community; kindness of others helps us heal from loss.

steps.title: Solved answers
steps.body:
**Q1. Why was the narrator unhappy at the start of high school? (2 marks)** He missed his old school and friends, felt lost in the new environment and was still grieving for his grandmother.

**Q2. What does the title mean? (3 marks)** A house is just a structure; a home is made by the love, care and support of family and community — which the narrator experienced after losing his house.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Don't say the narrator was injured badly — the focus is on loss and support.
- The help came from **schoolmates and the community**.

steps.title: Helping someone in crisis
steps.body: When a classmate faces loss (fire, flood, bereavement), practical help — books, notes, a meal, company — often matters more than words. If someone seems very low for a long time, encourage them to talk to a trusted adult or counsellor (Tele-MANAS **14416**).

activity.prompt: What makes your house a 'home'? List three things that are not objects.
activity.hint: Think of people, routines, memories, the way you feel there.

quiz.why: In 'A House Is Not a Home', the narrator was in the first year of high school when the fire happened. He was a freshman.
The house burned down in a fire. It is the central event in the story.
Schoolmates and the community helped the narrator and his family after the fire. This showed support.

quiz.q: Which pet was lost and later found?
quiz.why: The lost pet was a cat, which was found later. It brought joy.

options: A home is made by love and support
quiz.why: The theme is that a home is made by love and support, not just the building. That is the meaning of the title.

scenes.text: A drunk beggar tells a lawyer a sad, false story. Angry, the lawyer offers him work chopping wood.
Years later the beggar reveals that it was not the work but the kind cook, Olga, who changed his life.

steps.title: Summary (in our own words)
steps.body:
**Lushkoff**, a beggar, approaches **Sergei**, a lawyer, with a story of losing his job. Sergei recognises him as the same man who had told him a different story the day before. Angry, Sergei calls him a liar; Lushkoff admits it but says no one gives him work. Sergei offers him the job of **chopping wood** at his house.

The cook **Olga** takes Lushkoff to the woodshed; he is weak and drunk. Olga scolds him, **weeps**, and then **chops the wood herself**, while Lushkoff sits. Sergei, unaware, keeps sending Lushkoff more work and later helps him get a job copying papers. Lushkoff leaves, and Sergei is pleased he has 'reformed' him.

**Two years later**, Sergei meets Lushkoff at a theatre ticket window; he is now a **notary**, well dressed. Lushkoff thanks Sergei — but says it was really **Olga** who saved him: her kindness, her tears and her self-sacrifice made him give up drinking and change his life.

steps.title: Themes
steps.body:
- **Compassion transforms**: kindness, not lectures, changes people.
- **Dignity of labour**.
- **Irony**: Sergei thinks he reformed Lushkoff; actually Olga did.

steps.title: Solved long answer
steps.body:
**Q. Who was responsible for Lushkoff's transformation? (6 marks)**
Sergei believed his offer of work had reformed Lushkoff, and in part his help gave Lushkoff a chance. But the real change came from Olga, the cook. She scolded him, wept for his wasted life and secretly chopped the wood for him every time. Her selfless kindness moved Lushkoff deeply; he felt ashamed and stopped drinking. Thus Olga's compassion, more than Sergei's charity, transformed him.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Olga** chopped the wood, not Lushkoff.
- Lushkoff later became a **notary**.

activity.prompt: Sergei or Olga?

items.text: Got Lushkoff a job copying papers
Wept for Lushkoff and scolded him

quiz.why: The beggar's name in Chekhov's story was Lushkoff. He later reformed.
Sergei was a lawyer, who helped the beggar by sending him to chop wood. He thought he had reformed him.
Olga, Sergei's cook, chopped the wood, not Lushkoff. She was the one who did the real work.
Lushkoff later became a notary, a respectable job. It was Olga's kindness that changed him.
Anton Chekhov wrote 'The Beggar'. Wilde, Tolstoy and O. Henry wrote other works.

questions.q: Who wrote 'The Happy Prince'?
questions.why: Oscar Wilde wrote 'The Happy Prince'. O. Henry wrote 'The Last Leaf' and Chekhov 'The Beggar'.

questions.q: Toto was a:
questions.why: Toto was a pet monkey, in Ruskin Bond's story. He was not a dog or a cat.

questions.q: Who painted the last leaf?
questions.why: Behrman painted the last leaf on the wall, which saved Johnsy. It was his masterpiece.

questions.q: In 'The Beggar', the cook is:
questions.why: In 'The Beggar', the cook is Olga. Kezia and Margie belong to other stories, and Sue is from 'The Last Leaf'.

questions.q: Iswaran worked as a:
questions.why: Iswaran worked as a cook. He also told stories.

questions.q: In the kingdom of fools, people worked:
questions.why: In the kingdom of fools, people worked at night and slept by day. This shows the oddity of the place.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The lost child refused the stranger's gifts. Reason (R): He wanted only his parents.
options: Both true; R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The lost child refused the stranger's gifts because he wanted only his parents.

questions.q: Which story has a twist ending?
questions.why: 'The Last Leaf' by O. Henry has a twist ending, as Behrman painted the leaf. The other stories do not have this twist.

questions.q: Which two stories show selfless sacrifice for others?
options: Lost Child and Kingdom of Fools
The Happy Prince and The Last Leaf
questions.why: In 'The Happy Prince' the Prince and the swallow give up everything, and in 'The Last Leaf' Behrman gives his life. Both show selfless sacrifice.

questions.q: Why did Grandfather sell Toto?
options: Toto was too destructive and costly
questions.why: Grandfather sold Toto because he was too destructive and costly. He caused too much damage.

questions.q: Toto was bought for ₹5 and sold for ₹3. What was the loss percentage?
questions.why: Loss = 5 − 3 = ₹2, and loss % = 2 ÷ 5 × 100 = 40%. Percentage loss is taken on the cost price.

questions.q: Case: A student says Sergei reformed Lushkoff. What is the best correction?
options: Olga's compassion was the real cause of his change
questions.why: Sergei did not reform Lushkoff; it was Olga's compassion that really changed him. The irony is that Sergei took credit.

questions.q: What common lesson do 'A House Is Not a Home' and 'The Lost Child' share?
options: Love and belonging matter more than material things
questions.why: Both stories show that love and belonging matter more than material things. A house is more than a building, and the lost child wants his parents.

questions.q: Why did the guru's trick work on the king?
options: The foolish king believed he would be reborn as king
questions.why: The guru's trick worked because the foolish king believed he would be reborn as king if he was killed on the stake. Only a foolish king would believe it.

questions.q: Which statement best describes Iswaran's storytelling technique?
questions.why: Iswaran's storytelling used suspense, dramatic pauses and exaggeration to hold his listener. It was not flat or factual.

courses.title: Grammar · Tenses
courses.summary: All twelve tense forms — present, past and future in simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous — with time markers, solved examples, gap-filling and editing tasks in board format.
outcomes: Learners can form and use all twelve tense forms
Learners can choose tenses using time markers
Learners can maintain tense consistency in paragraphs
Learners can correct tense errors in editing tasks

scenes.text: Riya works at a café. She opens it at 7 every day (habit).
Right now she is baking muffins (in progress). She has baked 50 already (completed by now). She has been baking since 6 (continuing).

steps.title: Four present forms
steps.body:
- **Simple present** (V1 / V1+s): habits, facts, timetables. *The sun rises in the east. She walks to school.*
- **Present continuous** (am/is/are + V-ing): action now, temporary, planned future. *They are playing now.*
- **Present perfect** (has/have + V3): past action with present result; experience; *just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for*. *I have finished my homework.*
- **Present perfect continuous** (has/have been + V-ing): action began in past and still continuing; *since/for*. *She has been studying for two hours.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. Water ___ (boil) at 100°C. → **boils** (fact).
2. Look! The baby ___ (sleep). → **is sleeping** (now).
3. I ___ (not see) him since Monday. → **have not seen** (since → perfect).
4. They ___ (wait) for the bus for 30 minutes. → **have been waiting** (duration continuing).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using present perfect with a **definite past time**: ✗ *I have seen him yesterday* → ✓ *I saw him yesterday.*
- Stative verbs (know, like, believe, own) are not usually in continuous: ✗ *I am knowing* → ✓ *I know.*
- Third person singular needs **-s**: *He goes*, not *He go*.

steps.title: Time markers
steps.body: always/usually/every day → simple present · now/at the moment/look! → present continuous · just/already/yet/ever → present perfect · since/for (still going) → present perfect continuous.

activity.prompt: Fill in the correct present tense
activity.text: She ___ (live) in Pune. At the moment she ___ (read) a novel. She ___ (already finish) two chapters. She ___ (read) since morning.

quiz.why: A universal fact uses the simple present, and 'earth' is third person singular, so the verb is 'revolves'. 'Revolve' is wrong for a singular subject.
'Listen!' shows the action is happening now, so we use the present continuous: 'is knocking'.
'Three times' refers to experience up to now, so we use the present perfect: 'have seen'.
'Since 4 p.m.' shows an action that began in the past and is still going on, so we use the present perfect continuous: 'have been playing'.
'Know' is a stative verb, not normally used in continuous tenses, so 'I know the answer' is correct. 'Knowing' and 'am knowing' are wrong.

scenes.text: Yesterday, Aman was doing homework when the power went off.
By the time his mother found candles, he had already finished maths. He had been working for an hour.

steps.title: Four past forms
steps.body:
- **Simple past** (V2): completed action at a definite past time. *I met her yesterday.*
- **Past continuous** (was/were + V-ing): action in progress at a past moment; often interrupted. *I was reading when he called.*
- **Past perfect** (had + V3): the earlier of two past actions. *The train had left before we reached.*
- **Past perfect continuous** (had been + V-ing): action continued up to a past point. *She had been waiting for an hour when the bus came.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. Columbus ___ (discover) America in 1492. → **discovered**.
2. While I ___ (cross) the road, I ___ (see) an accident. → **was crossing**, **saw**.
3. When the police arrived, the thief ___ (escape). → **had escaped**.
4. He was tired because he ___ (run) for an hour. → **had been running**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- After *did*, use V1: ✗ *Did you went?* → ✓ *Did you go?*
- Don't use past perfect when there is only one past action and no sequence needed.
- Irregular V2/V3: go–went–gone; write–wrote–written; begin–began–begun.

steps.title: Sequence clue
steps.body: Two past actions: earlier one → **had + V3**; later one → **V2**. *After she had eaten, she went out.*

activity.prompt: Fill in the correct past tense
activity.text: When I ___ (reach) the station, the train ___ (already leave). I ___ (wait) for the next one when my friend ___ (call) me.

quiz.why: 'Last week' is a definite past time, so we use the simple past: 'went'. The present perfect is not used with a finished time.

quiz.q: I ___ TV when the phone rang.
quiz.why: A longer action (watching TV) was interrupted by a shorter one (the phone rang), so the longer one is in the past continuous: 'was watching'.

quiz.q: The patient ___ before the doctor came.
quiz.why: The patient's death happened earlier than the doctor's arrival, so the earlier action takes the past perfect: 'had died'.
After 'did', the main verb stays in its base form, so 'write' is correct. 'Wrote' and 'written' are wrong after 'did'.

quiz.q: They ___ for hours when the rescue team arrived.
quiz.why: The walking continued up to the point when the team arrived in the past, so we use the past perfect continuous: 'had been walking'.

scenes.text: Neha says, 'I'm going to visit Shimla. My train leaves at 6 tomorrow.'
'This time next week I will be skiing. By Sunday I will have finished my project.'

steps.title: Future forms
steps.body:
- **Simple future** (will/shall + V1): prediction, promise, instant decision. *It will rain.*
- **Future continuous** (will be + V-ing): action in progress at a future time. *At 8 p.m. I will be studying.*
- **Future perfect** (will have + V3): completed before a future time; *by*. *By June she will have graduated.*
- **Future perfect continuous** (will have been + V-ing): duration up to a future point. *By 2030 he will have been working here for ten years.*
- **Going to**: plan/intention; evidence. *Look at the clouds — it's going to rain.*
- **Present continuous for arrangements**; **simple present for timetables**: *The train leaves at 6.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. I think India ___ (win) the match. → **will win** (prediction).
2. Don't call at 9 — I ___ (sleep). → **will be sleeping**.
3. By next month, we ___ (complete) the bridge. → **will have completed**.
4. The flight ___ (depart) at 10:30 tomorrow. → **departs** (timetable).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In time/condition clauses (when, if, as soon as, before), use **present**, not will: ✗ *When he will come, I will tell him* → ✓ *When he comes, I will tell him.*
- Don't write *will can* → *will be able to*.

activity.prompt: Choose the correct future form
activity.text: Look at those clouds! It ___ (rain). By the time you arrive, I ___ (cook) dinner. If it ___ (rain), we will stay home.

quiz.why: A promise about the future uses 'will': 'will help'. 'Am helped' is a wrong passive.
'By 2030' gives a future deadline, so we use the future perfect: 'will have finished'.
In a time clause about the future, we use the simple present, not 'will'. So 'comes' is correct.

quiz.q: The school bus ___ at 7:15 every day.
quiz.why: A fixed timetable or habit uses the simple present: 'leaves'. 'Every day' signals a regular event.

quiz.q: This time tomorrow I ___ to Goa.
quiz.why: 'This time tomorrow' describes an action in progress at a future time, so we use the future continuous: 'will be flying'.

scenes.text: Ms Rao returns essays full of red marks: 'He go to school and played football yesterday.'
She teaches a trick: underline every verb and check its time.

steps.title: Consistency
steps.body: Stay in one time frame unless the meaning changes. Narratives → past; facts/instructions → present; reports of general truths can stay present (*He said the earth is round*).

steps.title: Solved editing task (board format)
steps.body:
Each line has one error. Write the incorrect word and the correction.
1. Yesterday I *go* to the market. → go / **went**
2. I *have bought* vegetables an hour ago. → have bought / **bought**
3. While I *walk* home, it started raining. → walk / **was walking**
4. I *reach* home after it had stopped. → reach / **reached**
5. My mother *cook* dinner now. → cook / **is cooking**

steps.title: Solved gap-filling paragraph
steps.body:
Ravi (a) ___ (wake) up late today. He (b) ___ (miss) the bus, so he (c) ___ (walk) to school. By the time he arrived, the assembly (d) ___ (end).
→ (a) **woke** (b) **missed** (c) **walked** (d) **had ended**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing present and past in one narrative without reason.
- 'Ago' with present perfect ✗.
- Forgetting the auxiliary in continuous forms (*She reading* ✗).

statements.s: 'I have finished it yesterday' is correct.
statements.why: Definite past time → 'I finished it yesterday'.

statements.s: 'When he comes, I will tell him' is correct.
'She has been living here since 2015' is correct.
'Did she went home?' is correct.

quiz.q: Correct the error: 'He go to school yesterday.'
quiz.why: 'Yesterday' shows past time, so the verb must be in the simple past: 'He went to school yesterday.' 'Go' is wrong.

quiz.q: Correct: 'I have seen him two days ago.'
quiz.why: 'Ago' goes with a finished past time, so the simple past 'saw' is correct, not the present perfect.

quiz.q: Choose: 'By the time we reached, the film ___.'
quiz.why: The film started before 'we reached', so the earlier action takes the past perfect: 'had started'.

quiz.q: Choose: 'She ___ in this school for five years now.'
quiz.why: 'For five years now' shows an action that began in the past and continues, so we use the present perfect continuous: 'has been teaching'.

quiz.q: A narrative story should mostly be in:
quiz.why: A narrative tells events that have already happened, so it is mostly in the past tense. Random mixing would confuse the reader.

questions.q: The sun ___ in the west.
questions.why: The sun's setting in the west is a general fact, so we use the simple present: 'sets'.

questions.q: They ___ football now.
questions.why: 'Now' shows the action is going on at the moment, so we use the present continuous: 'are playing'.

questions.q: She ___ a letter yesterday.
questions.why: 'Yesterday' marks the past, so we use the simple past: 'wrote'.

questions.q: I ___ my keys. I can't find them.
questions.why: Losing the keys has a present result (I can't find them), so we use the present perfect: 'have lost'.

questions.q: We ___ dinner when the guests arrived.
questions.why: The dinner was in progress when the guests arrived, so the past continuous 'were having' fits.

questions.q: By next year he ___ his degree.
questions.why: 'By next year' is a future deadline, so we use the future perfect: 'will have completed'.

questions.q: If it ___ tomorrow, the match will be cancelled.
questions.why: In an 'if' clause about the future, we use the simple present, not 'will'. So 'rains' is correct.

questions.q: She was tired because she ___ all day.
questions.why: She was tired because of work that went on for a long time before that moment, so we use the past perfect continuous: 'had been working'.

questions.q: Identify the error: 'He has went to Mumbai.'
questions.why: 'Has' needs the past participle, so 'has went' should be 'has gone'. 'Went' is the simple past.

questions.q: Choose: 'I ___ him since we were children.'
questions.why: 'Since we were children' shows a state continuing up to now, so we use the present perfect: 'have known'. 'Know' is a stative verb.

questions.q: Edit: 'When I reached the hall, the speaker already left.'
questions.why: The speaker's leaving happened before 'I reached', so the earlier action needs the past perfect: 'had already left'.

questions.q: Choose the correctly consistent sentence:
options: She opens the door and saw a cat.
She has opened the door and saw a cat.
She opened the door and saw a cat.
She opened the door and sees a cat.
questions.why: Both actions are in the past, so both verbs must be in the simple past: 'opened' and 'saw'. Mixing tenses is incorrect.

questions.q: By 2030 she ___ here for 20 years.
questions.why: 'By 2030' and 'for 20 years' show an action continuing up to a future point, so we use the future perfect continuous: 'will have been working'.

questions.q: Gap-fill: 'The teacher said that honesty ___ the best policy.'
questions.why: A universal truth stays in the present tense even in reported speech, so 'is' is correct.

questions.q: Edit the passage line: 'Every morning she wake up early, but today she overslept.'
questions.why: 'Every morning' shows a habit, and 'she' is third person singular, so the verb should be 'wakes'.

courses.title: Grammar · Modals and Determiners
courses.summary: Modals for ability, permission, possibility, obligation, necessity and advice; and determiners — articles, demonstratives, possessives and quantifiers — with solved gap-fills and editing.
outcomes: Learners can choose modals according to function
Learners can use modals in past forms (could have, should have)
Learners can use a/an/the and zero article correctly
Learners can use quantifiers like some, any, much, many, few, little

scenes.text: Arjun asks, 'Can I go out?' The teacher smiles: 'You can — you have legs. But may you? Ask politely.'
The class laughs and learns the difference between ability and permission.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
Modals: can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must, ought to; semi-modals: need, dare, used to, have to.
- A modal is followed by **V1** (base form): *She can swim* (not *can swims*).
- No -s for third person; no 'to' after most modals (except *ought to, have to, used to*).

**Ability**: can (present), could (past), be able to (all tenses). *I can drive. I could swim at five.*
**Permission**: may (formal), can (informal), could (polite). *May I come in?*
**Possibility**: may/might/could (uncertain), can (general). *It may rain. He might be late.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. ___ I borrow your pen? (polite) → **May/Could**.
2. My grandmother ___ read without glasses even at 80. → **can**.
3. Take an umbrella; it ___ rain. → **may/might**.
4. When I was young, I ___ climb trees easily. → **could**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *He can sings* → ✓ *He can sing.*
- ✗ *I will can come* → ✓ *I will be able to come.*
- 'Might' shows **less** certainty than 'may'.

activity.prompt: Fill in a suitable modal
activity.text: ___ I use your phone, please? She ___ speak four languages. It ___ snow tonight, so carry a jacket.

quiz.why: 'May' is used for formal permission, as in 'May I come in, sir?'. 'Must' and 'should' do not ask for permission.

quiz.q: She ___ play the violin when she was six.
quiz.why: 'Could' shows ability in the past, as 'when she was six'. 'Can' is for the present.
A modal verb is followed by the base form of the verb, so 'He can sing' is correct. 'Can sings' and 'can to sing' are wrong.
'Might' expresses a possibility, something that may happen but is not certain. It does not show ability or obligation.
'Can' has no future form, so we use 'will be able to' for future ability. 'Will can' is incorrect.

scenes.text: A sign says: 'You must shower before swimming. You mustn't run. You needn't bring a towel — we provide one.'
The coach adds: 'You should drink water. You ought to stretch first.'

steps.title: Uses
steps.body:
- **Must**: strong obligation (often from speaker), certainty/deduction. *You must wear a helmet. He must be tired (deduction).*
- **Have to**: external obligation. *I have to wear a uniform.* Past: *had to.*
- **Mustn't**: prohibition. *You mustn't smoke here.*
- **Needn't / don't have to**: no necessity. *You needn't hurry.*
- **Should / ought to**: advice, duty. *You should apologise.*
- **Should have + V3**: past regret/criticism. *You should have told me.*
- **Shall**: offers/suggestions with I/we. *Shall we go?*
- **Would**: polite requests, past habit. *Would you help me? He would walk daily.*
- **Used to**: past habit/state no longer true. *I used to live in Agra.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. Students ___ wear uniforms on Mondays. (rule) → **must/have to**.
2. You ___ shout in the library. (prohibition) → **mustn't**.
3. It's a holiday; you ___ come to school. → **needn't / don't have to**.
4. You look pale; you ___ see a doctor. → **should**.
5. The lights are off; they ___ be asleep. → **must** (deduction).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- *Mustn't* (forbidden) ≠ *needn't* (not necessary).
- ✗ *You should went* → ✓ *You should have gone.*
- *Must* has no past form for obligation — use *had to*.

activity.prompt: What does the modal express?

items.text: You must wear a seat belt.
You mustn't use phones in the exam hall.
You needn't bring lunch; it's provided.
You should sleep early before exams.
We have to submit the form by Friday.

quiz.q: You ___ park here; it's a no-parking zone.
quiz.why: 'Mustn't' shows prohibition, which is what a no-parking zone means. 'Needn't' only means it is not necessary.

quiz.q: You ___ buy a ticket; entry is free.
quiz.why: 'Needn't' means it is not necessary to buy a ticket, as entry is free. 'Mustn't' would mean it is forbidden.

quiz.q: I missed the bus. I ___ left earlier.
quiz.why: 'Should have' shows regret about a past action, that leaving earlier would have been right. 'Would' and 'can' don't fit.
'Must' has no past form of its own, so we use 'had to' for past obligation.

quiz.q: 'He must be at home; his car is outside' shows:
quiz.why: 'Must be' here is a logical conclusion from the clue (his car is outside). That is deduction, not obligation or permission.

scenes.text: Kabir writes 'a owl' and 'an university'. His teacher circles both.
'Listen to the sound, not the letter,' she says. 'An owl. A university.'

steps.title: Articles
steps.body:
- **a/an** (indefinite): singular countable nouns, first mention, any one. **a** before consonant **sound** (*a university, a one-rupee coin, a European*); **an** before vowel **sound** (*an hour, an honest man, an MBA, an umbrella*).
- **the** (definite): known/specific, already mentioned, unique (*the sun*), superlatives (*the best*), ordinals (*the first*), rivers/oceans/mountain ranges (*the Ganga, the Himalayas*), newspapers (*The Hindu*), musical instruments (*play the guitar*).
- **Zero article**: general plural/uncountable (*Milk is healthy*), names of people/most countries/cities, meals, games, languages, subjects (*She plays cricket. We study history.*).

steps.title: Demonstratives and possessives
steps.body:
- **this/these** (near), **that/those** (far): *this book, those trees*.
- **Possessives**: my, your, his, her, its, our, their — *its* (no apostrophe) is possessive; *it's* = it is.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. She is ___ honest girl. → **an** (silent h).
2. ___ Ganga is a holy river. → **The**.
3. He is ___ European. → **a** (sounds 'yoo').
4. I had ___ breakfast at 8. → **(no article)**.
5. This is ___ best day of my life. → **the** (superlative).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *a hour* → ✓ *an hour*; ✗ *an university* → ✓ *a university*.
- ✗ *The Mount Everest* → ✓ *Mount Everest* (single peaks: no article), but *the Himalayas*.
- ✗ *its* vs *it's* confusion.

activity.prompt: Fill in a, an, the — or write 0 for no article
activity.text: I saw ___ elephant at ___ zoo. It was ___ biggest animal there. My brother wants to join ___ university in Delhi.

quiz.why: 'Hour' begins with a silent h, so it starts with a vowel sound and takes 'an': 'an hour'.
'The' is used with the names of mountain ranges, so 'The Himalayas' is correct.
'MBA' starts with the vowel sound 'em', so it takes 'an': 'an MBA'. It's the sound that counts, not the letter.
No article is used before the names of games, so 'play cricket' is correct.
'Its' is the possessive of 'it' and has no apostrophe. 'It's' means 'it is'.

scenes.text: Mom says, 'We have little sugar left, a few eggs and not much milk.'
Riya notes: buy some sugar, many eggs — and asks, 'Is there any bread?'

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- **many** (countable plural) / **much** (uncountable): *many books, much water* (much mostly in negatives/questions).
- **a lot of / lots of**: both.
- **few** (hardly any, negative sense) / **a few** (some, positive) — countable: *A few friends came* (some); *Few people came* (almost none).
- **little / a little** — uncountable: *I have a little money* (some); *There is little hope* (almost none).
- **some** (positive sentences, offers/requests) / **any** (negatives, questions): *Would you like some tea? I don't have any time.*
- **each** (individually, singular noun), **every** (all, singular noun), **either/neither** (two).
- **several, enough, all, both, no**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. There isn't ___ milk in the fridge. → **much/any**.
2. ___ students passed; most failed. → **Few**.
3. I have ___ friends in Mumbai, so I won't be lonely. → **a few**.
4. ___ of the two roads leads to the station. → **Either/Neither** (by meaning).
5. ___ child got a gift. → **Every/Each**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *much books* → ✓ *many books*.
- ✗ *less people* → ✓ *fewer people* (countable).
- *Each/every* + **singular** verb: *Every student has a book.*

activity.prompt: Match the quantifier to its use

quiz.why: Sugar is uncountable, so we use 'much': 'How much sugar'. 'Many' is for countable nouns.

quiz.q: There were ___ people at the show; it was almost empty.
quiz.why: 'Few' (without 'a') means hardly any, matching the sense that the show was almost empty. 'A few' means some.
In offers we use 'some', as in 'Would you like some juice?'. 'Any' is used in questions and negatives.
'Every' takes a singular verb, so 'Every student has a uniform' is correct.

quiz.q: Choose: '___ cars are on the road today than yesterday.'
quiz.why: 'Cars' is countable, so we use 'fewer'. 'Less' is for uncountable nouns.

questions.q: She ___ speak French fluently.
questions.why: A modal like 'can' is followed by the base form, with no 's' or 'to', so 'She can speak' is correct.

questions.q: He is ___ honest man.
questions.why: 'Honest' begins with a silent h, so it has a vowel sound and takes 'an': 'an honest man'.

questions.q: How ___ books do you have?
questions.why: 'Books' is countable, so we use 'many'. 'Much' and 'little' are for uncountable nouns.

questions.q: You ___ not tell lies.
questions.why: 'Should' gives moral advice. 'You should not tell lies' says it's wrong to lie.

questions.q: ___ we go for a walk?
questions.why: 'Shall we...?' is used to make a suggestion or offer, as in 'Shall we go for a walk?'.

questions.q: I have ___ money, enough for a snack.
questions.why: 'A little' means some, enough for a snack. 'Little' alone would mean almost none.

questions.q: Choose: 'You ___ come tomorrow; the meeting is cancelled.'
questions.why: 'Needn't' means it is not necessary to come, as the meeting is cancelled. 'Mustn't' would mean you are forbidden.

questions.q: ___ Taj Mahal is in Agra.
questions.why: 'The' is used with a unique monument or structure, so 'The Taj Mahal' is correct.

questions.q: Identify the error: 'He must to finish the work.'
questions.why: 'Must' is followed directly by the base verb, with no 'to'. So 'must to' should be 'must'.

questions.q: Choose: 'She ___ have reached by now; she left an hour ago.'
questions.why: 'Should have reached' expresses what is expected, since she left an hour ago. 'Needn't' and 'mustn't' don't fit.

questions.q: Edit: 'I have less friends than my brother.'
questions.why: 'Friends' is countable, so we use 'fewer', not 'less'. Less is for uncountable nouns.

questions.q: Choose: 'You ___ have told me earlier; I could have helped.'
questions.why: 'Should have told me earlier' is a past criticism: you did not tell me, but it would have been right to. 'Can' and 'will' don't fit.

questions.q: Choose: 'He is ___ one-eyed man.'
questions.why: 'One' begins with a 'w' sound, which is a consonant sound, so we use 'a': 'a one-eyed man'.

questions.q: Gap-fill: '___ of the two answers is correct; both are wrong.'
questions.why: 'Neither' means not one of the two, which fits the idea that both answers are wrong. 'Either' would mean one of them.

questions.q: Choose the sentence with correct modal use:
options: I use to lived in Pune.
I used to living in Pune.
I used to live in Pune.
questions.why: 'Used to' is followed by the base form of the verb: 'I used to live in Pune'. The other versions break this rule.

school-c9-english-d.title: Class 9 English · Grammar II, Reading, Writing & Revision
school-c9-english-d.description: Class 9 English skills: subject–verb agreement, active and passive voice, reported speech, unseen passages, descriptive paragraphs, diary entries and story writing — plus a Revision & Practice course with two mock papers.

courses.title: Grammar · Subject–Verb Agreement and Voice
courses.summary: Rules of subject–verb concord (including tricky subjects) and how to change sentences between active and passive voice in all common tenses.
outcomes: Learners can apply the basic and advanced rules of subject–verb agreement
Learners can identify and correct agreement errors
Learners can convert active to passive voice in all common tenses
Learners can choose voice appropriately in writing

scenes.text: Sana writes: 'The box of chocolates are on the table.' Her friend frowns.
'What is on the table — the box or the chocolates?' 'The box!' 'So: the box ... is.'

steps.title: Core rules
steps.body:
1. A **singular subject** takes a singular verb; a **plural subject** a plural verb. *The boy plays. The boys play.*
2. Find the **real subject**; ignore phrases in between: *The box of chocolates **is** on the table. The leader, along with his followers, **was** arrested.* (with, along with, as well as, together with, besides don't change the subject.)
3. Two subjects joined by **and** → plural: *Ram and Shyam are friends.* But if they refer to **one person/idea** → singular: *Bread and butter is my breakfast. The poet and singer has come.*
4. **Either…or / neither…nor / not only…but also**: verb agrees with the **nearer** subject: *Neither the teacher nor the students **were** present. Either the students or the teacher **is** coming.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. The quality of these apples ___ (is/are) poor. → **is** (subject: quality).
2. My friend, as well as his parents, ___ (is/are) coming. → **is**.
3. Neither Raju nor his friends ___ (was/were) late. → **were** (nearer: friends).
4. Rice and dal ___ (is/are) a common meal. → **is** (one dish).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Agreeing with the noun nearest to the verb instead of the real subject (*The list of items **are*** ✗).
- Using plural with 'as well as' subjects.

activity.prompt: Choose is/are or was/were
activity.text: The bunch of keys ___ missing. Neither the manager nor the clerks ___ in the office. My sister, together with her friends, ___ going to the fair.

quiz.q: The colour of the flowers ___ beautiful.
quiz.why: The subject is 'colour', which is singular, so the verb is 'is'. 'Of the flowers' is only a phrase.
Two people joined by 'and' make a plural subject, so the verb is 'are'.

quiz.q: Either you or he ___ to go.
quiz.why: With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'he', so we use 'has'.

quiz.q: The captain, with his team, ___ arrived.
quiz.why: 'With his team' does not change the subject, which is 'the captain', so the verb is singular: 'has'.
'Slow and steady' is one idea (a single quality), so it takes a singular verb: 'wins'.

scenes.text: 'The news are good!' says Rohan.
His mother smiles: 'News is uncountable — the news is good.'

steps.title: Rules for tricky subjects
steps.body:
- **Each, every, everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, either, neither** → singular: *Each of the boys **has** a bag. Everyone **is** here.*
- **Collective nouns** (team, family, jury, committee): singular when acting as a unit (*The team **is** strong*); plural when members act individually (*The jury **are** divided*).
- **Uncountable nouns** → singular: news, information, furniture, advice, luggage.
- **Plural-looking nouns** with singular meaning: mathematics, physics, economics, measles, news → singular. *Mathematics **is** my favourite.*
- **Always plural**: scissors, trousers, spectacles, cattle, police, people. *The police **are** coming.* (*A pair of scissors **is**...*)
- **Amounts/distance/time as one unit** → singular: *Ten kilometres **is** a long walk. Five hundred rupees **is** enough.*
- **The number of** → singular; **a number of** → plural. *The number of students **is** 40. A number of students **are** absent.*
- **One of + plural noun** → singular verb: *One of my friends **lives** in Pune.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. Physics ___ (is/are) interesting. → **is**.
2. The cattle ___ (is/are) grazing. → **are**.
3. A number of people ___ (was/were) injured. → **were**.
4. Each of the girls ___ (has/have) a prize. → **has**.
5. Fifty rupees ___ (is/are) too much for this pen. → **is**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *The furnitures are* → ✓ *The furniture is*.
- ✗ *One of my friend live* → ✓ *One of my friends lives*.
- 'Police' is **plural** in standard usage.

activity.prompt: Singular or plural verb?

quiz.why: 'News' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb: 'The news is shocking'.
'Each' is singular, so the verb is 'has'. 'Of them' doesn't change that.
'The number of' takes a singular verb, since 'number' is the subject. So 'is increasing' is correct.
'Trousers' is always plural, so it takes 'are'. We say 'my trousers are torn'.
'One of the boys' has the singular subject 'one', so the verb is 'is'.

lessons.title: Active and passive voice: forming the passive

scenes.text: A reporter writes: 'Someone stole a rare painting from the museum.'
The editor changes it: 'A rare painting was stolen from the museum.' The painting matters more than the unknown thief.

steps.title: How to form the passive
steps.body:
**Active**: subject does the action — *The cat chased the mouse.*
**Passive**: subject receives the action — *The mouse was chased by the cat.*
Steps: object → subject · use correct form of **be** + **V3** · subject → 'by + agent' (often omitted if unknown/unimportant) · keep the **tense** same.

| Tense | Passive form |
- Simple present: am/is/are + V3 → *Letters are written.*
- Present continuous: am/is/are being + V3 → *A letter is being written.*
- Present perfect: has/have been + V3 → *The work has been done.*
- Simple past: was/were + V3 → *The house was built in 1990.*
- Past continuous: was/were being + V3 → *The road was being repaired.*
- Past perfect: had been + V3 → *The thief had been caught.*
- Simple future: will be + V3 → *The results will be announced.*
- Modals: modal + be + V3 → *This must be done.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. She writes a poem. → **A poem is written by her.**
2. They are building a bridge. → **A bridge is being built (by them).**
3. Someone has stolen my bike. → **My bike has been stolen.**
4. The teacher will check the papers. → **The papers will be checked by the teacher.**
5. You must follow the rules. → **The rules must be followed.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing the tense: ✗ *She wrote a letter → A letter is written* → ✓ *A letter was written.*
- Pronoun forms: *by him/her/them*, not *by he/she/they*.
- Intransitive verbs (no object) **cannot** be passive: *He sleeps* has no passive.

activity.prompt: Change to passive (fill the verb phrase)
activity.text: They repair cars here. → Cars ___ here. She has cooked dinner. → Dinner ___ by her. The police caught the thief. → The thief ___ by the police.

options: The door is opened by him
The door was opened by him
quiz.why: In the simple present passive, the object becomes the subject: 'The door is opened by him.' The tense is kept.

quiz.q: Passive of 'They are painting the wall':
options: The wall is being painted by them
quiz.why: The present continuous passive is 'is/are being + past participle', so 'The wall is being painted by them' is correct.

quiz.q: Passive of 'She will sing a song':
options: A song will be sung by her
A song is sung by her
quiz.why: The future passive is 'will be + past participle': 'A song will be sung by her'.

quiz.q: Which sentence cannot be made passive?
quiz.why: 'He laughed' has no object, so it is intransitive and cannot be made passive. The other sentences have objects.
After 'by' we use the object form, so 'by she' becomes 'by her'. 'Herself' is a reflexive pronoun.

lessons.title: Using passive in writing; editing practice

scenes.text: Kunal writes: 'I took a beaker. I poured water.' His science teacher says reports usually use the passive.
He rewrites: 'A beaker was taken. Water was poured into it.' Now it sounds like a proper report.

steps.title: When to use passive
steps.body:
- When the **doer is unknown** or unimportant: *My phone was stolen.*
- In **scientific/process writing**: *The solution is heated to 60°C.*
- In **news/notices**: *The school will be closed on Monday.*
- To focus on the **receiver** of the action.
Use active for direct, lively writing (stories, letters).

steps.title: Solved process paragraph (passive)
steps.body: **How tea is made**: First, water is boiled in a pan. Then tea leaves are added and the mixture is boiled for two minutes. Milk and sugar are added according to taste. Finally, the tea is strained into cups and served hot.

steps.title: Solved editing (agreement + voice)
steps.body:
1. The list of names *are* on the board. → are / **is**
2. The letters *was* posted yesterday. → was / **were**
3. A new library *is build* in our school. → is build / **is being built** (or **has been built**)
4. Everyone *have* submitted the form. → have / **has**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting 'be' in passive (*The cake baked by her* ✗ in passive sense → *The cake was baked by her*).
- Overusing passive in stories, making them dull.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of the process (passive voice)
items: Water is boiled in a pan
Tea leaves are added
The mixture is boiled for two minutes
Milk and sugar are added
The tea is strained and served

options: The doer is unknown or unimportant
quiz.why: The passive is preferred when the doer is unknown or unimportant, so the focus is on the action. It is less lively than the active.
'Yesterday' needs the past, and the parcel is singular, so the past passive is 'was delivered'.
'Everyone' is singular, so it takes 'has': 'Everyone has finished.'
Process writing uses the passive voice in the present tense, as it describes steps without naming who does them. It sounds impersonal.
'Now' shows the action is going on, so we use the present continuous passive: 'is being built'.

questions.q: She ___ to school every day.
questions.why: 'She' is third person singular, so the simple present verb takes -s: 'goes'.

questions.q: The children ___ playing.
questions.why: 'Children' is plural, so with 'playing' the helping verb is 'are'.

questions.q: Passive of 'I cleaned the room':
options: The room was cleaned by me
The room is cleaned by me
questions.why: The past active becomes the past passive: 'The room was cleaned by me'.

questions.q: Mathematics ___ difficult for some.
questions.why: 'Mathematics' is singular in form, so it takes 'is'. It is a subject name, not plural.

questions.q: Neither the boys nor the girl ___ ready.
questions.why: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the girl', so we use 'is'.

questions.q: Passive of 'They have finished the work':
options: The work has been finished by them
questions.why: The present perfect passive is 'has/have been + past participle': 'The work has been finished by them'.

questions.q: A number of students ___ absent today.
questions.why: 'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb, so 'are' is correct. 'The number of' would take a singular verb.

questions.q: Passive of 'Who wrote this book?'
options: By whom was this book written?
This book is written by who?
questions.why: A question in the active 'Who wrote this book?' becomes 'By whom was this book written?' in the passive.

questions.q: The jury ___ divided in their opinions.
questions.why: The jury is divided in their opinions, so the members act individually and the verb is plural: 'are'.

questions.q: Edit: 'The furnitures in the room is new.'
questions.why: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and has no plural form, so 'furnitures' is wrong. Then 'is' also fits correctly.

questions.q: Passive of 'You should respect elders':
questions.why: A modal passive uses 'modal + be + past participle': 'Elders should be respected'.

questions.q: Passive of 'The workers were repairing the road':
options: The road was being repaired by the workers
questions.why: The past continuous passive is 'was/were being + past participle': 'The road was being repaired by the workers'.

questions.q: Choose: 'The Prime Minister, along with his ministers, ___ the summit.'
questions.why: The subject is 'The Prime Minister', singular, and 'along with his ministers' doesn't change it. So we use 'attends'.

questions.q: Choose the correct sentence:
options: Five hundred rupee is a big amount.
Five hundred rupees is a big amount.
Five hundred rupees were a big amounts.
Five hundred rupees are a big amount.
questions.why: An amount of money is treated as one unit and takes a singular verb. 'Five hundred rupees is a big amount' is correct.

questions.q: Passive of 'Let him do it':
options: Let it be done by him
Let it is done by him
questions.why: The passive of 'Let him do it' is 'Let it be done by him'. The object 'it' becomes the subject.

courses.title: Grammar · Reported Speech
courses.summary: How to report statements, questions, commands and requests: tense back-shift, pronoun and time/place changes, reporting verbs, and the gap-fill format used in board exams.
outcomes: Learners can report statements with correct back-shift
Learners can report yes/no and wh-questions
Learners can report commands, requests and advice
Learners can complete dialogue-based reporting tasks

scenes.text: Dad calls: 'I am stuck in traffic. I will be late.'
Priya tells Mom, 'Dad said that he was stuck in traffic and that he would be late.'

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
**Direct**: She said, "I am tired." → **Indirect**: She said that she was tired.
1. **Reporting verb**: said → said/told (told + object). *He told me that…*
2. **Tense back-shift** (if reporting verb is past): present → past; past → past perfect; present perfect → past perfect; will → would; can → could; may → might; shall → should.
3. **Pronouns** change by sense: I → he/she; we → they; my → his/her.
4. **Time/place**: now → then; today → that day; yesterday → the previous day / the day before; tomorrow → the next day / the following day; here → there; this → that; ago → before.
5. **No back-shift** for universal truths or when reporting verb is present: *The teacher said that the earth revolves round the sun.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. He said, "I am playing." → He said that he **was playing**.
2. She said, "I have finished my work." → She said that she **had finished** her work.
3. Ravi said to me, "I will meet you tomorrow." → Ravi told me that he **would meet me the next day**.
4. Mom said, "I bought this yesterday." → Mom said that she **had bought that the previous day**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *He told that…* → ✓ *He told me that…* / *He said that…*
- Forgetting to change pronouns and time words.
- Back-shifting universal truths ✗.

activity.prompt: Complete the reported speech
activity.text: Direct: She said, "I am going to the market today." Indirect: She said that she ___ going to the market ___.

quiz.q: He said, "I like tea." → He said that he ___ tea.
quiz.why: In reported speech the present tense shifts back to the past: 'like' becomes 'liked'.
'Tomorrow' changes to 'the next day' in reported speech. 'The previous day' is for 'yesterday'.

quiz.q: She said, "I can swim." → She said that she ___ swim.
quiz.why: 'Can' changes to 'could' in reported speech, as the reporting verb is in the past.

quiz.q: The teacher said, "Water boils at 100°C." → The teacher said that water ___ at 100°C.
quiz.why: A universal truth stays in the present tense even in reported speech, so 'boils' stays.

options: He told that he was ill
He told me that he was ill
He said to that he was ill
He said me that he was ill
quiz.why: 'Tell' needs an object, as in 'He told me that...'. 'Said' does not take a direct object like 'me'.

scenes.text: At an interview, the panel asks Zoya, 'Where do you live? Have you used Excel?'
Later she writes in her diary: 'They asked me where I lived and whether I had used Excel.'

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Reporting verb: **asked, enquired, wanted to know, wondered**.
- **Yes/No questions**: use **if/whether**. *He said, "Are you ready?" → He asked if I was ready.*
- **Wh-questions**: keep the wh-word. *She said, "Where do you live?" → She asked where I lived.*
- Change question order to **statement order** (subject before verb); remove 'do/does/did'; no question mark.
- Apply tense back-shift and pronoun/time changes.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. He said to me, "Do you like music?" → He asked me **if I liked** music.
2. She said, "What are you doing?" → She asked **what I was doing**.
3. The teacher said, "Why were you late?" → The teacher asked **why I had been late**.
4. Mom said, "Will you help me?" → Mom asked **whether I would help her**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *She asked where did I live* → ✓ *She asked where I lived.*
- ✗ *He asked that if I was ready* — don't use 'that' with questions.
- Don't put a question mark at the end.

activity.prompt: Report the questions
activity.text: "Are you hungry?" she asked. → She asked ___ I was hungry. "Where is the station?" he asked. → He asked where the station ___.

quiz.q: He said, "Can you drive?" → He asked ___ I could drive.
quiz.why: A yes/no question is reported with 'if' or 'whether': 'He asked if I could drive.'

quiz.q: She said, "Why are you crying?" → She asked why I ___ crying.
quiz.why: In a reported question we use statement order and shift the tense back, so 'are crying' becomes 'was crying'.

options: He asked where did she go
He asked that where she went
He asked where she had gone
quiz.why: A reported question uses statement word order and a back-shift, so 'where did she go' becomes 'where she had gone'.
A reported question is a statement in form, so it ends with a full stop, not a question mark.

quiz.q: "Have you eaten?" → She asked whether I ___ eaten.
quiz.why: The present perfect 'have eaten' shifts back to the past perfect 'had eaten' in reported speech.

scenes.text: Coach shouts: 'Run faster! Don't stop!'
Later Arjun tells his mother, 'The coach ordered us to run faster and told us not to stop.'

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Use **told/ordered/commanded** (commands), **requested/asked** (requests), **advised** (advice), **warned**, **suggested**.
- Structure: reporting verb + **object** + **to + V1**. Negative: **not to + V1**.
- *He said to me, "Close the door." → He told me to close the door.*
- *She said, "Please help me." → She requested me to help her.*
- *The doctor said, "Don't eat junk food." → The doctor advised me not to eat junk food.*
- **Let's** → **suggested that we should** + V1: *He said, "Let's go out." → He suggested that we should go out.*
- **Exclamations**: *He said, "What a lovely day!" → He exclaimed that it was a very lovely day.*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. The teacher said, "Sit down." → The teacher **ordered/told us to sit down**.
2. Mom said, "Please bring some milk." → Mom **requested me to bring** some milk.
3. He said, "Don't touch the wire." → He **warned me not to touch** the wire.
4. Riya said, "Let's play chess." → Riya **suggested that we should play** chess.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- ✗ *He told me don't go* → ✓ *He told me not to go.*
- ✗ *requested to me* → ✓ *requested me*.
- 'Please' disappears — use 'requested'.

activity.prompt: Match the direct speech to the reporting verb

quiz.q: He said, "Open the window." → He told me ___ the window.
quiz.why: A command is reported with 'told + object + to + base verb': 'He told me to open the window.'

quiz.q: She said, "Don't shout." → She told us ___ shout.
quiz.why: A negative command is reported as 'told + object + not to + base verb', so 'not to shout' is correct.

quiz.q: "Please give me water," said the old man. → The old man ___ me to give him water.
quiz.why: 'Please' shows the old man is making a request, so the reporting verb is 'requested'. 'Ordered' would fit a command.

quiz.q: "Let's start," said Raj. → Raj ___ that we should start.
quiz.why: 'Let's' is a suggestion, so it is reported with 'suggested that we should...'.

quiz.q: The doctor said, "Take rest." → The doctor ___ me to take rest.
quiz.why: 'Take rest' from a doctor is advice, so the reporting verb is 'advised'. 'Warned' would suggest danger.

scenes.text: Doctor: 'How long have you had this cough?' Patient: 'For a week.' Doctor: 'Drink warm water.'
The exam asks: complete the report of this dialogue. Students who know the patterns finish in two minutes.

steps.title: Solved dialogue task
steps.body:
**Dialogue**
Teacher: Why didn't you complete your homework?
Rohan: I was unwell yesterday.
Teacher: Submit it by tomorrow.

**Report** (fill blanks):
The teacher asked Rohan (a) **why he had not completed his homework**. Rohan replied that (b) **he had been unwell the previous day**. The teacher then (c) **told/ordered him to submit it by the next day**.

steps.title: Solved second task
steps.body:
**Dialogue**
Aisha: Mom, can I go to Riya's party?
Mom: Have you finished your project?
Aisha: Yes, I finished it this morning.

**Report**: Aisha asked her mother (a) **if she could go to Riya's party**. Her mother asked (b) **whether she had finished her project**. Aisha replied (c) **that she had finished it that morning**.

steps.title: Exam checklist
steps.body:
1. Reporting verb fits the type (asked/replied/told/requested/advised).
2. Back-shift tense.
3. Change pronouns and time words.
4. Statement word order for questions.
5. Fit the blank's grammar exactly (check what comes before/after).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing more words than the blank allows.
- Using 'said' for every line — vary: replied, enquired, exclaimed, added.

activity.prompt: Report the dialogue
activity.text: Shopkeeper: "What do you want?" → The shopkeeper asked me what I ___. Me: "I need a pen." → I replied that I ___ a pen.

quiz.q: "I was ill yesterday," he said. → He said that he ___ ill the previous day.
quiz.why: The simple past 'was' shifts to the past perfect 'had been' in reported speech, and 'yesterday' becomes 'the previous day'.

quiz.q: "Submit it tomorrow." → She told me to submit it ___.
quiz.why: 'Tomorrow' becomes 'the next day' in reported speech.

quiz.q: "Can I go?" asked Aisha. → Aisha asked if she ___ go.
quiz.why: 'Can' becomes 'could' in reported speech, so 'Aisha asked if she could go.'

quiz.q: Which reporting verb suits an answer to a question?
quiz.why: 'Replied' is the reporting verb for an answer to a question. 'Ordered' and 'warned' don't fit.
'This morning' becomes 'that morning' in reported speech, as 'this' changes to 'that'.

questions.q: He said, "I am happy." → He said that he ___ happy.
questions.why: In reported speech, 'am' shifts back to 'was': 'He said that he was happy.'

questions.q: 'Here' changes to:
questions.why: 'Here' changes to 'there' in reported speech, as the place shifts.

questions.q: She said, "Sit down." → She told me ___ down.
questions.why: A command is reported with 'told + object + to + verb': 'She told me to sit down.'

questions.q: He said, "I will come." → He said that he ___ come.
questions.why: 'Will' changes to 'would' in reported speech, so 'He said that he would come.'

questions.q: She said, "Are you okay?" → She asked ___ I was okay.
questions.why: A yes/no question is reported using 'if' or 'whether': 'She asked if I was okay.'

questions.q: 'Yesterday' changes to:
questions.why: 'Yesterday' changes to 'the previous day' in reported speech.

questions.q: "Where do you work?" he asked. → He asked where I ___.
questions.why: A reported question uses statement order, and the present 'work' shifts to the past: 'where I worked'. We don't use 'did' again.

questions.q: "Don't be late," said the teacher. → The teacher told us ___ late.
questions.why: A negative command is reported as 'told us not to be late'. It uses 'not to' before the base verb.

questions.q: "Let's play cricket," said Amit. → Amit ___.
options: suggested that we should play cricket
questions.why: 'Let's' is a suggestion, so it is reported as 'suggested that we should play cricket'. It is not an order or request.

questions.q: "I have lost my wallet," she said. → She said that she ___ her wallet.
questions.why: The present perfect 'have lost' shifts to the past perfect 'had lost' in reported speech.

questions.q: Choose the correct report: Ravi said, "The sun rises in the east."
options: Ravi said the sun had risen
Ravi said that the sun rises in the east
Ravi said that the sun rose in the east
questions.why: A universal truth stays in the present tense, so 'the sun rises in the east' remains unchanged in reported speech.

questions.q: Report: "What a beautiful painting!" said Meena.
options: Meena asked what a beautiful painting
Meena exclaimed that it was a very beautiful painting
questions.why: An exclamation is reported with 'exclaimed that...', and the tense shifts back. 'What a beautiful painting!' becomes 'it was a very beautiful painting'.

questions.q: "Did you see the match?" he asked me. → He asked me ___.
options: whether I had seen the match
questions.why: A yes/no question is reported with 'whether' or 'if', and 'did you see' shifts to 'I had seen' in the past perfect.

questions.q: "Please help me with this bag," the lady said to me. Best report:
options: The lady asked that please help
The lady requested me to help her with that bag
The lady ordered me to help her with that bag
The lady said me to help
questions.why: 'Please' makes it a request, so the reporting verb is 'requested', and 'this' becomes 'that'. 'Ordered' would be wrong.
